docs.title: ucode-prometheus-exporter
docs.text:
Metrics of OpenWrt for Prometheus, written in ucode and served by uhttpd at /metrics on port 9100. It replaces the packages feed's prometheus-node-exporter-ucode and prometheus-node-exporter-lua. It ports the Lua exporter's collectors alongside the ucode one's, under names of its own: the package is ucode-prometheus-exporter, and the service, command and configuration are prometheus-exporter.

apk add ucode-prometheus-exporter ucode-prometheus-exporter-full
wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1:9100/metrics
  • node_exporter's names. Where the Prometheus node_exporter has a metric, the exporter writes its name, type, labels and help, so dashboards made for node_exporter work. Other metrics follow the Prometheus naming conventions.
  • A collector per package. The base package has the collectors every device can use. Each other collector is a package of its own, and groups install several at once.
  • A jail built from what the collectors declare. uhttpd runs the exporter in procd's jail, which holds what the installed collectors need and nothing else.
  • Nothing to observe is not a failure. A device without radios, or with dnsmasq disabled, is not failing to read them.
  • A ubus object and a LuCI app. Ask the exporter what it would do, from a script or from LuCI.

It targets OpenWrt 25.12, and uses no ucode API newer than that release's. Apache License 2.0.

docs.title: Renamed Metrics
docs.text:
This exporter replaces OpenWrt's prometheus-node-exporter-ucode and prometheus-node-exporter-lua. It conflicts with both and takes over their settings, but not their metric names.

Where the Prometheus node_exporter has an equivalent metric, this exporter uses node_exporter's name, type, labels and help text. So dashboards made for node_exporter (such as Grafana's "Node Exporter Full") work. Elsewhere, the names follow the Prometheus naming conventions:

  • base units in the name (_seconds, _bytes, _hertz, _bits_per_second, _celsius, _ratio, and _dbm or _db for radio levels)
  • _total on counters only, and every counter ends in _total
  • a metric made only of labels is <name>_info, with the value 1
  • a boolean is a gauge of 0 or 1; an enumeration is one series per state, with the value 1 or 0
  • snake_case metric and label names, and no unit on a unitless value

Each service keeps its own prefix (adguard_, dnsmasq_, dsl_, wireguard_, mwan3_, hostapd_, dawn_, bmx7_, realtek_poe_, ubnt_, modemmanager_, unbound_, nft_counter_). OpenWrt's own metrics are node_openwrt_*. Some services have a widely used standalone exporter whose names follow the conventions. For those, this exporter uses the standalone exporter's names: see Standalone exporters.

No option brings the old names back. The tables below list, per collector, every family whose name, type, labels or unit changed. Each row goes from the name in the exporters this one replaces to this exporter's name. A family that is not listed kept its name. In the Type column, a → b is a type that changed.

See also:

  • Metrics, for every family as the collectors write it now
  • Migrate from prometheus-node-exporter-lua/-ucode, for every family of the feed's exporters and this exporter's equivalent
  • About metric names, for why the names are what they are

docs.title: Base collectors
docs.text:
Before After Type Why node_cpu_seconds_total{cpu="cpu0",mode} node_cpu_seconds_total{cpu="0",mode} counter node_exporter labels the CPU by its number. node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="guest"\|"guest_nice"} node_cpu_guest_seconds_total{mode="user"\|"nice"} counter node_exporter keeps guest time apart (the kernel counts it in user and nice as well). node_procs_running_total node_procs_running gauge A gauge has no _total; node_exporter's name. node_procs_blocked_total node_procs_blocked gauge A gauge has no _total; node_exporter's name. node_memory_<Field>_bytes of a field without a unit (HugePages_Total, HugePages_Free, HugePages_Rsvd, HugePages_Surp) node_memory_<Field> gauge Page counts, not bytes: node_exporter names them without a unit. Fields in kB keep _bytes. node_selinux_enabled, node_selinux_current_mode unchanged gauge node_exporter's help texts. — node_network_receive_nohandler_total{device} counter New: node_exporter's netdev collector reads it from netlink too. — node_network_up{device} gauge New: node_exporter's, 1 when the operstate is up. node_network_info{device,address,broadcast,duplex,operstate,ifalias} node_network_info{device,address,broadcast,duplex,operstate,adminstate,ifalias} gauge node_exporter's labels: adminstate is up or down by the IFF_UP flag. node_network_speed_bytes (left out at 0 Mb/s) node_network_speed_bytes (0 Mb/s is 0) gauge As node_exporter, which leaves out only an unknown speed (-1).

conntrack, entropy, filefd, loadavg, time and uname already had node_exporter's names.

docs.title: Network collectors
docs.text: Before After Type Why node_netstat_<Section>_<Field> (from /proc/net/netstat and /proc/net/snmp) node_netstat_<Section>_<Field> gauge → untyped node_exporter's type, and its help text Statistic <Section><Field>. By default only the fields node_exporter's --collector.netstat.fields keeps, some 40 of about 400; the option fields, a regular expression, takes others (.* for every one). snmp6_<Name>{device="all"} (from /proc/net/snmp6) node_netstat_<Protocol>_<Field> (node_netstat_Ip6_InReceives, node_netstat_Icmp6_*, node_netstat_Udp6_*, node_netstat_UdpLite6_*) counter → untyped node_exporter's netstat collector reads /proc/net/snmp6; written by the netstat collector, not snmp6. snmp6_<Name>{device} (from /proc/net/dev_snmp6/<device>) node_snmp6_<Protocol>_<Field>_total{device} counter node_exporter has no per-device IPv6 statistics: the node_ namespace, the name split as netstat splits it, and _total on a counter. By default only 13 fields of a device's 70 or so: its octets, ICMP messages and errors, the datagrams it forwarded, discarded or found no route for, and those it received with a bad header, address or size; the option fields, a regular expression of <Protocol>_<Field>, takes others (.* for every one). snmp6_ifIndex{device} node_snmp6_ifindex{device} counter → gauge An interface index is not a count. Not in the default fields: netclass's node_network_iface_id{device} is the same index. node_ethtool_<stat> node_ethtool_<stat> untyped node_exporter's naming: rx and tx are spelled out only between underscores (rx0_x stays rx0_x), a statistic is named Network interface <stat>, a device's statistics are written sorted by name, and every statistic of a name two of them make is left out (before, the first was kept). Only the links a device backs (/sys/class/net/<link>/device) are asked: not bridges, VLANs, WireGuard, ifb or veth, whose drivers have no statistics or repeat netdev's. node_ethtool_{received,transmitted}_*_total (7 common statistics) unchanged untyped node_exporter's help texts (Network interface bytes received, ...). — node_ethtool_info{bus_info,device,driver,expansion_rom_version,firmware_version,version} gauge New: node_exporter's, from ethtool -i <device>. — node_network_supported_port_info{device,type}, node_network_{supported,advertised}_speed_bytes{device,duplex,mode}, node_network_{autonegotiate,pause,asymmetricpause}_{supported,advertised}{device}, node_network_autonegotiate{device} gauge New: node_exporter's ethtool collector's link information, from ethtool <device>: each link mode 1000baseT/Full as mode="1000baseT",duplex="full", in bytes per second, pause frames and autonegotiation 0 or 1. The link's speed and duplex are netclass's node_network_speed_bytes and node_network_info, as they are node_exporter's netclass collector's. node_nat_traffic{src,dest} node_nat_traffic_bytes{host}; node_nat_traffic_bytes{host,peer} with the option peers gauge Base unit in the name. A gauge: a sum over the connections there are now. By host on this side of the router (the source of a connection, or the LAN host a port forward reaches), which a LAN bounds: a series per pair of addresses came and went with every connection. peers adds the address at the other end, off by default for that churn. nft_counter_packets nft_counter_packets_total counter A counter ends in _total. nft_counter_bytes nft_counter_bytes_total counter A counter ends in _total.

docs.title: Wireless collectors
docs.text:
wifi writes the families of node_exporter's wifi collector, with its help texts and labels: device (was ifname) and mac_address (was mac). It adds a radio label to every family. Its option stations, on by default, writes the station metrics. The Lua exporter wrote those in a separate wifi_stations collector, which this exporter has not had since 0.2.0.

Before After Type Why wifi_radio_info{radio,htmode,channel,country} node_wifi_radio_info{radio,htmode,channel,country} gauge node_exporter's node_wifi_ namespace. — node_wifi_interface_frequency_hertz{radio,device} gauge New: node_exporter's. wifi_network_info{radio,ifname,ssid,bssid,mode} node_wifi_network_info{radio,device,ssid,bssid,mode} gauge node_wifi_ namespace, node_exporter's device label. wifi_network_quality (percent) node_wifi_network_quality_ratio gauge A ratio, not a percentage. wifi_network_bitrate (kbit/s) node_wifi_network_transmit_bits_per_second gauge Base unit. wifi_network_noise_dbm node_wifi_network_noise_dbm gauge node_wifi_ namespace. wifi_network_signal_dbm node_wifi_network_signal_dbm gauge node_wifi_ namespace. — node_wifi_channel_{active,busy,receive,transmit}_seconds_total{radio,device} counter New, from the survey of the interface's channel (NL80211_SURVEY_INFO_TIME, _BUSY, _RX, _TX, in ms), in seconds; node_exporter has no such metric. Per interface, as the noise: the interfaces of one radio repeat its counts. A time the driver does not count is left out. wifi_stations_total{radio,ifname} (wifi), wifi_stations{ifname} (Lua's wifi_stations) node_wifi_stations{radio,device} counter → gauge (wifi) The stations associated now are not a counter; wifi's stations writes them. — node_wifi_station_connected_seconds_total counter New: node_exporter's. wifi_station_inactive_milliseconds node_wifi_station_inactive_seconds gauge node_exporter's name, in seconds. wifi_station_receive_kilobits_per_second node_wifi_station_receive_bits_per_second gauge node_exporter's name, in bits per second. wifi_station_transmit_kilobits_per_second node_wifi_station_transmit_bits_per_second gauge node_exporter's name, in bits per second. wifi_station_receive_bytes_total node_wifi_station_receive_bytes_total counter node_exporter's name. wifi_station_transmit_bytes_total node_wifi_station_transmit_bytes_total counter node_exporter's name. wifi_station_signal_dbm node_wifi_station_signal_dbm gauge node_exporter's name. — node_wifi_station_transmit_retries_total, node_wifi_station_transmit_failed_total, node_wifi_station_beacon_loss_total counter New: node_exporter's, where the driver reports them. wifi_station_transmit_packets_total node_wifi_station_transmitted_packets_total counter node_exporter's name. wifi_station_receive_packets_total node_wifi_station_received_packets_total counter node_exporter's name. wifi_station_expected_throughput_kilobits_per_second node_wifi_station_expected_throughput_bits_per_second gauge Base unit, node_wifi_ namespace. dawn_ap_stations_total dawn_ap_stations gauge A gauge has no _total. hostapd_station_*{vif,ssid,bssid,encryption,frequency,channel,station} hostapd_station_*{vif,station} unchanged The network's labels are on the info metric below: a channel change (DFS, ACS) no longer starts a new series of every station's counters. — (labels of hostapd_station_*) hostapd_station_info{vif,station,ssid,bssid,encryption,frequency,channel} gauge The station's network, as an info metric, one per station.

The hostapd_ubus_stations families already followed the conventions and are unchanged.

docs.title: Hardware and system collectors
docs.text:
Before After Type Why node_hwmon_*{chip} node_hwmon_*{chip} gauge node_exporter's chip names: each part lowercased with every character but a-z, 0-9, : and _ an underscore (platform_nct6775.656 is platform_nct6775_656), and chips that would share a name told apart by their name file or hwmonN. node_hwmon_chip_names{chip,chip_name} unchanged gauge chip_name cleaned as node_exporter does; written only for chips with a name file. node_exporter's help. node_hwmon_sensor_label, node_hwmon_temp_celsius, node_hwmon_pwm unchanged gauge node_exporter's help texts. node_thermal_zone_temp{zone,type,policy,mode,passive} node_thermal_zone_temp{zone,type} gauge node_exporter's labels and help; a mode change no longer starts a new series. — (labels of node_thermal_zone_temp) node_thermal_zone_info{zone,type,policy,mode} gauge The policy and mode, as an info metric. — (label passive, in millidegrees) node_thermal_zone_passive_celsius{zone,type} gauge The passive trip point as a value, in degrees. node_os_info unchanged gauge node_exporter's help text. — node_os_version{id,name} gauge New: node_exporter's, the major.minor of the release (none for a snapshot). dhcp_host_info{name,mac,ip} (ucode) node_openwrt_dhcp_host_info{name,mac,ip} gauge In OpenWrt's own namespace. uci_dhcp_host{name,dns,ip,duid,mac} (Lua) node_openwrt_dhcp_host_info{name,mac,ip} gauge As the ucode exporter's: dns and duid are not written.

filesystem and textfile already had node_exporter's names; node_openwrt_info is unchanged.

docs.title: dnsmasq
docs.text: Before After Type Why dnsmasq_<key>_total of a counter (dns_*, dhcp_*, bootp, pxe, noanswer, leases_*) unchanged gauge → counter They count up from dnsmasq's start. dnsmasq_dnssec_max_crypto_use_total, dnsmasq_dnssec_max_sig_fail_total, dnsmasq_dnssec_max_work_total dnsmasq_dnssec_max_crypto_use, dnsmasq_dnssec_max_sig_fail, dnsmasq_dnssec_max_work gauge High-water marks, not counters: no _total. dnsmasq_tcp_connections_total dnsmasq_tcp_connections gauge The TCP connections open now. dnsmasq_<key>_total of a key a later dnsmasq adds dnsmasq_<key> gauge → untyped Not known to be a counter.

docs.text:
Before After Type Why dsl_up{detail} dsl_up gauge A boolean without a label that changes with the state. — (label detail of dsl_up) dsl_state_info{state} gauge The driver's state of the line, as an info metric. dsl_aggregated_transmit_power_db{direction} dsl_aggregated_transmit_power_dbm{direction} gauge A power, in dBm. dsl_datarate{direction} dsl_data_rate_bits_per_second{direction} gauge Base unit in the name. dsl_max_datarate{direction} dsl_max_data_rate_bits_per_second{direction} gauge Base unit in the name.

docs.title: wireguard
docs.text: Before After Type Why wireguard_sent_bytes_total{public_key} wireguard_sent_bytes_total{interface,public_key,allowed_ips,friendly_name} gauge → counter prometheus_wireguard_exporter's labels and help. wireguard_received_bytes_total{public_key} wireguard_received_bytes_total{interface,public_key,allowed_ips,friendly_name} gauge → counter prometheus_wireguard_exporter's labels and help. wireguard_latest_handshake_seconds{public_key} wireguard_latest_handshake_seconds{interface,public_key,allowed_ips,friendly_name} gauge prometheus_wireguard_exporter's labels and help. wireguard_interface_info{name,public_key,listen_port,fwmark} wireguard_interface_info{interface,public_key,listen_port,fwmark} gauge interface, as in the other families; an unset fwmark is left out, not NaN. wireguard_peer_info{interface,public_key,description,endpoint,persistent_keepalive_interval} wireguard_peer_info{interface,public_key,friendly_name,endpoint,persistent_keepalive_interval} gauge friendly_name, as in the other families, and only with the collector's peer_names (the old one always had description); an unset keepalive is left out, not NaN.

docs.title: mwan3
docs.text:
Before After Type Why mwan3_interface_age mwan3_interface_age_seconds counter → gauge Seconds since the last check: goes back to 0. mwan3_interface_online mwan3_interface_online_seconds counter → gauge Goes back to 0 when the interface goes offline. mwan3_interface_offline mwan3_interface_offline_seconds counter → gauge Goes back to 0 when the interface comes online. mwan3_interface_uptime mwan3_interface_uptime_seconds counter → gauge An uptime, with its unit. mwan3_interface_lost unchanged counter → gauge Probes lost in the current check. mwan3_interface_turn unchanged counter → gauge Rounds in the current check.

mwan3_interface_score, _status (one series per state), _enabled, _running and _up are unchanged.

docs.title: bmx7
docs.text: Before After Type Why bmx7_status{id,name,address,revision} bmx7_info{id,name,address,revision} gauge A metric of labels only is _info. bmx7_cpu_usage (percent) bmx7_cpu_usage_ratio gauge A ratio. bmx7_mem_usage bmx7_memory_usage_bytes gauge Base unit in the name. bmx7_link_rxRate{source,target,name,dev} bmx7_link_receive_rate_bits_per_second{source,target,name,device} gauge snake_case, base unit, the usual device label. bmx7_link_txRate{source,target,name,dev} bmx7_link_transmit_rate_bits_per_second{source,target,name,device} gauge snake_case, base unit, the usual device label. bmx7_tunIn{name,network} bmx7_tun_in_info{name,network} gauge snake_case, _info. bmx7_plugin{name} bmx7_plugin_info{name} gauge _info.

docs.title: modemmanager
docs.text: Before After Type Why modemmanager_signal_quality (percent) modemmanager_signal_quality_ratio gauge A ratio. modemmanager_signal_<tech>_<measure> modemmanager_signal_<tech>_<measure>_<unit>: _dbm for rssi, rsrp, rscp and io, _db for rsrq, snr, sinr and ecio, _seconds for the refresh rate; none for a measure not known gauge Unit in the name.

docs.title: ubnt-manager
docs.text:
Every family is a gauge (ubnt_uptime and ubnt_timestamp were counters) labeled device.

Before After Why labels hostname,devmodel,fwversion,essid of ubnt_uptime ubnt_info{device,hostname,devmodel,fwversion,essid} The radio's names, as an info metric. ubnt_uptime ubnt_uptime_seconds Unit; a gauge. ubnt_timestamp ubnt_time_seconds The radio's clock: a gauge, as node_time_seconds. ubnt_totalram, ubnt_freeram ubnt_memory_total_bytes, ubnt_memory_free_bytes Bytes (airOS 6 reports kB, airOS 8 bytes). ubnt_cpuload (percent) ubnt_cpu_load_ratio A ratio. ubnt_cpubusy, ubnt_cputotal ubnt_cpu_busy, ubnt_cpu_all No _total on a gauge. ubnt_temperature ubnt_temperature_celsius Unit. ubnt_frequency, ubnt_center1_freq, ubnt_chanbw (MHz) ubnt_frequency_hertz, ubnt_center1_frequency_hertz, ubnt_channel_width_hertz Base unit. ubnt_signal, ubnt_noisef, ubnt_txpower ubnt_signal_dbm, ubnt_noise_floor_dbm, ubnt_transmit_power_dbm Unit. ubnt_distance ubnt_distance_meters Unit. ubnt_txrate, ubnt_rxrate (Mbit/s) ubnt_transmit_rate_bits_per_second, ubnt_receive_rate_bits_per_second Base unit. ubnt_throughput_tx, ubnt_throughput_rx (kbit/s) ubnt_transmit_throughput_bits_per_second, ubnt_receive_throughput_bits_per_second Base unit. ubnt_polling_cb_capacity, _dl_capacity, _ul_capacity (kbit/s) ubnt_airmax_combined_capacity_bits_per_second, ubnt_airmax_downlink_capacity_bits_per_second, ubnt_airmax_uplink_capacity_bits_per_second Base unit. ubnt_use, ubnt_tx_use, ubnt_rx_use ubnt_airtime_use, ubnt_transmit_airtime_use, ubnt_receive_airtime_use Named for what they are; left as airOS reports them, their scale unknown. ubnt_count ubnt_stations Named for what it counts. ubnt_aprepeater, ubnt_rstatus ubnt_ap_repeater, ubnt_radio_status snake_case.

ubnt_loadavg, ubnt_channel, ubnt_band, ubnt_dfs, ubnt_rssi, ubnt_rx_chainmask, ubnt_tx_chainmask, ubnt_cac_state, ubnt_cac_timeout, ubnt_rx_idx, ubnt_rx_nss, ubnt_tx_idx, ubnt_tx_nss and ubnt_atpc_status keep their names.

docs.title: unbound
docs.text:

lacks there. unbound_requestlist_avg, unbound_requestlist_max unbound_request_list_avg{thread}, unbound_request_list_max{thread} gauge As unbound_exporter's other request list families. unbound_query_{tcp,tcpout,udpout,tls,tls_resume,https,ipv6,edns_present,edns_DO}_total, unbound_answers_{secure,bogus}_total, unbound_rrset_bogus_total, unbound_query_aggressive_nsec_total{rcode}, docs.title: New metrics
docs.text:
Neither upstream exporter had these. Where node_exporter has the metric, the name, type, labels and help are node_exporter's.

Collector Families Type Source — (the exporter's own) ucode_prometheus_exporter_build_info{version} gauge 1, labeled with the package's version (0.1.0-r1, dev from a source tree), in every scrape whatever collect[] selects; as node_exporter's node_exporter_build_info. — (the exporter's own) node_scrape_collector_observing{collector} gauge Beside node_exporter's node_scrape_collector_success: 0 for a collector with nothing to observe (its hardware, kernel feature or service is not there; it succeeds without samples), 1 for every other; see About nothing to observe. conntrack (base) node_nf_conntrack_stat_{found,invalid,ignore,insert,insert_failed,drop,early_drop,search_restart} gauge node_exporter's, from /proc/net/stat/nf_conntrack summed over the CPUs. softnet (base) node_softnet_{processed,dropped,times_squeezed,cpu_collision,received_rps,flow_limit_count}_total{cpu} counter node_exporter's, from /proc/net/softnet_stat. softnet (base) node_softnet_backlog_len{cpu} gauge node_exporter's. vmstat (base) node_vmstat_<field> (default fields: oom_kill, pgpg*, pswp*, pg*fault*; option fields) untyped node_exporter's, from /proc/vmstat. openwrt_interfaces (base) node_openwrt_interface_{up,pending,available,autostart}{interface} gauge netifd's network.interface dump, 0 or 1. openwrt_interfaces (base) node_openwrt_interface_uptime_seconds{interface} gauge netifd's uptime, while the interface is up. openwrt_interfaces (base) node_openwrt_interface_info{interface,proto,device,l3_device} gauge 1; a label netifd does not report is left out. openwrt_interfaces (base) node_openwrt_interface_addresses{interface,family}, node_openwrt_interface_routes{interface,family} gauge Counts: an address as a label would change with every WAN lease. openwrt_interfaces (base) node_openwrt_interface_ipv6_prefixes{interface}, node_openwrt_interface_errors{interface} gauge Delegated prefixes; the errors netifd holds for the interface. dhcp_leases node_openwrt_dhcp_leases{server,interface,family} gauge Active leases of dnsmasq (its lease file) and odhcpd (ubus call dhcp ipv4leases/ipv6leases). dhcp_leases (option leases) node_openwrt_dhcp_lease_info{server,interface,family,address,mac,duid,iaid,hostname}, node_openwrt_dhcp_lease_expiry_timestamp_seconds{server,interface,family,address} gauge A series per lease; off by default, for churn and privacy. timesync (base) node_timesync_synchronized{daemon} gauge 1 or 0, for each NTP daemon procd runs: ntpd (busybox, from its last event, kept by the base package's hotplug script: synchronized below stratum 16) and chronyd (chronyc -c tracking: synchronized unless its leap status is Not synchronised). node_exporter's node_timex_sync_status is the kernel's adjtimex(2) state, which ucode cannot read: not the same, so not its name. timesync (base) node_timesync_stratum{daemon}, node_timesync_offset_seconds{daemon}, node_timesync_last_update_timestamp_seconds{daemon} gauge While synchronized: the stratum, the offset at the last update (chronyd's last offset, ntpd's event's), and when that was (chronyd's reference time, ntpd's event) as a timestamp, as the conventions want a time since something. Not node_exporter's node_timex_offset_seconds, the offset the kernel still has to slew. chrony chrony_tracking_info{tracking_address,tracking_name,tracking_refid}, chrony_tracking_{last_offset_seconds,reference_timestamp_seconds,system_time_seconds,remote_reference,rms_offset_seconds,root_delay_seconds,root_dispersion_seconds,frequency_ppms,residual_frequency_ppms,skew_ppms,update_interval_seconds,stratum} gauge chrony_exporter's, from chronyc -c tracking. chrony chrony_sources_{last_sample_age_seconds,reachability_ratio,reachability_success,last_sample_offset_seconds,last_sample_error_margin_seconds,polling_interval_seconds,stratum}{source_address,source_name}, chrony_sources_state_info{source_address,source_name,source_state,source_mode} gauge chrony_exporter's, from chronyc -c sources. chrony chrony_serverstats_*_total (NTP, NTS-KE and command packets received and dropped, client log records dropped, authenticated and interleaved packets, timestamps by where they were taken), chrony_serverstats_ntp_timestamps_held, chrony_serverstats_ntp_timestamp_span_seconds counter, gauge chrony_exporter's, from chronyc -c serverstats, where chronyd serves time and its command socket can be reached: outside the exporter's jail (see How to monitor chrony). qdisc node_qdisc_{bytes,packets,drops,requeues,overlimits}_total{device,kind} counter node_exporter's (collector/qdisc_linux.go), from tc -s -j qdisc show: the root qdisc of each device, as node_exporter reports them; noqueue is left out. qdisc node_qdisc_current_queue_length{device,kind}, node_qdisc_backlog{device,kind} gauge node_exporter's: packets and bytes queued. qdisc node_qdisc_cake_capacity_estimate_bytes_per_second{device}, node_qdisc_cake_memory_used_bytes{device}, node_qdisc_cake_memory_limit_bytes{device} gauge A root CAKE qdisc's shaper rate and memory. No CAKE exporter is widely used: tc's JSON keys (tc/q_cake.c), in base units. qdisc node_qdisc_cake_tin_{bytes,packets,drops,ecn_marks,ack_drops}_total{device,tin} counter Per tin, tin its index as tc numbers them (0 for besteffort; 0 to 3, Bulk to Voice, for diffserv4). qdisc node_qdisc_cake_tin_{threshold_rate_bytes_per_second,backlog_bytes,peak_delay_seconds,average_delay_seconds,base_delay_seconds,sparse_flows,bulk_flows,unresponsive_flows}{device,tin} gauge Per tin; tc's delays in µs, here in seconds (base is tc's sp_delay, the sparse flows' delay). diskstats node_disk_{reads,writes}_completed_total{device}, node_disk_{reads,writes}_merged_total{device}, node_disk_read_bytes_total{device}, node_disk_written_bytes_total{device}, node_disk_{read,write}_time_seconds_total{device}, node_disk_io_time_seconds_total{device}, node_disk_io_time_weighted_seconds_total{device} counter node_exporter's (collector/diskstats_linux.go), from /proc/diskstats: sectors of 512 bytes in bytes, milliseconds in seconds. Devices the device_exclude option matches are left out: by default node_exporter's (RAM disks, zram, loop devices, the partitions of SCSI, virtio and NVMe disks) and flash (mtdblock, ubiblock) and the partitions and boot areas of an eMMC or SD card. diskstats node_disk_io_now{device} gauge node_exporter's: the I/Os in progress. diskstats node_disk_discards_{completed,merged}_total{device}, node_disk_discarded_sectors_total{device}, node_disk_discard_time_seconds_total{device}, node_disk_flush_requests_total{device}, node_disk_flush_requests_time_seconds_total{device} counter node_exporter's, where the kernel's line has them (discards since 4.18, flushes since 5.5); discarded sectors stay sectors, as there. diskstats node_disk_info{device,major,minor,rotational} gauge node_exporter's, without the labels it takes from udev's database (path, wwn, model, serial, revision), which OpenWrt does not have and which node_exporter leaves empty without it. hwmon node_hwmon_fan_rpm{chip,sensor}, node_hwmon_fan_min_rpm{chip,sensor}, node_hwmon_fan_alarm{chip,sensor} gauge node_exporter's, from a chip's fanN_input, _min and _alarm. hwmon node_hwmon_in_volts{chip,sensor}, node_hwmon_in_min_volts{chip,sensor}, node_hwmon_in_max_volts{chip,sensor}, node_hwmon_in_alarm{chip,sensor} gauge node_exporter's, from inN_input, _min, _max (mV, here volts) and _alarm. hwmon node_hwmon_curr_amps{chip,sensor}, node_hwmon_power_watt{chip,sensor} gauge node_exporter's, from currN_input (mA, here amperes) and powerN_input (µW, here watts). hwmon node_hwmon_temp_max_celsius{chip,sensor}, node_hwmon_temp_crit_celsius{chip,sensor}, node_hwmon_temp_alarm{chip,sensor} gauge node_exporter's, from tempN_max and tempN_crit (m°C, here degrees) and tempN_alarm: the limits a chip or its driver sets, as a radio's throttling thresholds. hwmon node_hwmon_power_average_watt{chip,sensor} gauge node_exporter's, from powerN_average (µW, here watts), where a power meter keeps an average. interrupts node_interrupts_total{cpu,type,info,devices} counter node_exporter's (collector/interrupts_linux.go), from /proc/interrupts: a series per interrupt and CPU, info a numbered interrupt's chip and devices the rest of its line, or a named one's description. node_exporter has it off by default, for those series: here a package of its own, in no group. filesystem node_filesystem_files{device,fstype,mountpoint}, node_filesystem_files_free{device,fstype,mountpoint} gauge node_exporter's, as the Lua exporter had them: the inodes and free inodes of each mount, from the package's rpcd object prometheus-exporter.filesystem, the statvfs() of the host's mounts. Where rpcd has not loaded it, the sizes alone. pressure node_pressure_{cpu,io,memory}_waiting_seconds_total, node_pressure_{cpu,io,memory,irq}_stalled_seconds_total counter node_exporter's (collector/pressure_linux.go), from /proc/pressure/*: the some and full lines' totals, µs in seconds; irq's full alone, where the kernel has it. It needs a kernel with CONFIG_PSI, which OpenWrt's leave off: here a package of its own, in no group, to install where the kernel has it. thermal node_cooling_device_cur_state{name,type}, node_cooling_device_max_state{name,type} gauge node_exporter's, of its thermal_zone collector, which reads them beside the zones: the throttle state of each cooling device of /sys/class/thermal (a fan, a CPU's frequency, a radio's duty cycle), name its number. sockstat node_sockstat_sockets_used, node_sockstat_<protocol>_{inuse,orphan,tw,alloc,mem,memory} (TCP, UDP, UDPLITE, RAW, FRAG, and TCP6, UDP6, UDPLITE6, RAW6, FRAG6 where the kernel has IPv6) gauge node_exporter's (collector/sockstat_linux.go), from /proc/net/sockstat and /proc/net/sockstat6, each key a protocol's line has. sockstat node_sockstat_<protocol>_mem_bytes gauge node_exporter's: mem, in pages, times the page size (the process's AT_PAGESZ, from /proc/self/auxv).

docs.title: Unchanged collectors
docs.text: conntrack (beyond the statistics above), entropy, filefd, filesystem, hostapd_ubus_stations, loadavg, realtek-poe, textfile, time and uname write the families they wrote before.

docs.title: Standalone exporters
docs.text: Service Exporter Followed? unbound letsencrypt/unbound_exporter Yes: its names, help texts and per-thread thread label, with _total added to the counters it names without (queries_discard_timeout, queries_wait_limit, queries_replyaddr_limit, dns_error_reports, and of the extended statistics answers_bogus, query_aggressive_nsec, rpz_action_count); its extended statistics, where unbound has extended-statistics: yes, the histogram unbound_response_time_seconds summed as it sums it. WireGuard prometheus_wireguard_exporter Yes: wireguard_sent_bytes_total, wireguard_received_bytes_total and wireguard_latest_handshake_seconds, its help texts and labels (interface, public_key, allowed_ips, friendly_name). chrony SuperQ/chrony_exporter Yes: its chrony_tracking_*, chrony_sources_* and chrony_serverstats_* names, help texts and labels; a source's source_name is its address, as it has it without DNS lookups (its default). Its _ppms names are kept: ppm is the unit chrony speaks in, and the base unit, a ratio, would make 33.8 ppm 3.38e-05. chrony_up is not: the scrape's node_scrape_collector_success is. A source never sampled has no chrony_sources_last_sample_age_seconds (chrony_exporter writes 4294967295). dnsmasq google/dnsmasq_exporter No: its counters (dnsmasq_hits, dnsmasq_misses, ...) have no _total and are typed as gauges, and they are the cache figures of dnsmasq's CHAOS TXT records, not the ubus call dnsmasq metrics this collector reads.

docs.title: About the Exporter
docs.text: ucode-prometheus-exporter serves the metrics of an OpenWrt device to Prometheus: its CPU, memory, network devices and connections, and the services a router runs, from Wi-Fi to WireGuard to DNS. It is written in ucode, OpenWrt's own scripting language, and served by uhttpd, the web server every OpenWrt image already has. This page is about where it comes from, and why it is a rewrite rather than a patch.

docs.title: Two exporters before it
docs.text:
OpenWrt's packages feed has had two Prometheus exporters, both Apache-2.0.

prometheus-node-exporter-lua came first, in 2017. Christian Simon added it; Etienne Champetier maintains it, and split its single script into the collectors it has today. Over the years contributors added collectors for nearly everything a router does: Wi-Fi stations, hostapd, DSL modems, PoE switches, mesh daemons, mwan3, ModemManager, Ubiquiti radios, Unbound.

prometheus-node-exporter-ucode followed in 2022, by Andre Heider, who maintains it. It is the same idea in ucode, which OpenWrt had by then made its language of choice: LuCI's backend and the firewall, fw4, are ucode, and rpcd takes plugins in it. It has the core collectors and a handful of extras, and needs no Lua.

Between them, the ground was covered twice and unevenly: most collectors existed in Lua only, a few in ucode only, and some in both with different names. A device that wanted the Lua exporter's breadth needed a Lua runtime, which an image built around ucode otherwise does without.

docs.title: Why a rewrite
docs.text:
This exporter ports the Lua exporter's collectors alongside the ucode one's, so every collector either exporter had is here, in ucode. Writing them anew, rather than translating them line by line, let every collector take the same shape. That shape is built for three things a router asks of code that runs on it: to touch only what it must, to be tested before it gets there, and to be fast on a MIPS CPU.

  • Each collector says what it touches. A collector declares the capabilities it needs, the configs it reads and the programs it runs, and gets those and nothing else. The service builds its jail from those declarations: see About the security model.
  • Everything is tested off the device. Only one module touches the system, and the tests hand collectors fakes of it, fed with what real devices answered. A collector is tested on the captures of real routers before it ever runs on one.
  • It is fast where it matters. A typical router's full scrape takes about 2.6 seconds on a MIPS CPU of 500 MIPS, the class of an MT7621. See Performance on small routers.
  • It says what it cannot observe. A device without radios is not failing to read its radios. See About nothing to observe.
  • The metric names are node_exporter's. Dashboards made for node_exporter work as they are. See About metric names.

The names are the change that costs the most: queries made for either feed exporter break. A rewrite is the time to pay that once, rather than have every later version carry two sets of names.

docs.title: Why not node_exporter itself
docs.text: The Prometheus node_exporter runs on Linux, and some run it on OpenWrt. But it is a Go binary of several megabytes, a lot on a router with 16 MB of flash. And it knows nothing of what makes a device an OpenWrt router: netifd's interfaces, hostapd, ubus, uci. This exporter takes node_exporter's names, so it fits the same dashboards, and adds what only OpenWrt has. Its base package takes about 120 KiB of flash (264 KiB installed), and an image with LuCI mostly has what it depends on, ucode and uhttpd, already.

docs.title: Replacing, not sitting beside
docs.text: It installs under names of its own, ucode-prometheus-exporter and the prometheus-exporter service. It conflicts with both feed exporters, since they all want port 9100 and uhttpd's /metrics. Installed where one of them was, it takes over that one's settings. See How to move from the feed's exporters.

docs.title: Credits
docs.text:
The collectors port those of the two feed packages: prometheus-node-exporter-ucode, by Andre Heider and contributors, and prometheus-node-exporter-lua, by Jeff Schornick, Kevin Lyda, Christian Simon, Etienne Champetier and contributors. NOTICE credits each collector's upstream authors.

Metric names and help texts follow the Prometheus node_exporter and, for Unbound, WireGuard and chrony, unbound_exporter, prometheus_wireguard_exporter and chrony_exporter. Tests run on utest.

docs.title: About the Architecture
docs.text: The exporter is not a daemon. It is a handler that uhttpd runs, a library of modules, a ubus object that rpcd serves, and an init script that ties them to procd. This page covers how those pieces fit, and why they are cut where they are.

docs.title: The pieces
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    P[Prometheus] -- "GET /metrics" --> U
    subgraph jail[procd's jail]
        U[uhttpd] --> H[handler.uc]
        H --> L[collectors]
    end
    L -- "deps: fs, ubus, uci, netlink, exec" --> S[(the system)]
    R[rpcd] --> O[ubus object prometheus-exporter]
    O --> LuCI
    O -.-> X[rpc-status.uc]
    I[init script] -- "jail.uc: mounts" --> jail
  • uhttpd and the handler. /usr/libexec/prometheus-exporter/handler.uc is a uhttpd-mod-ucode handler for /metrics. uhttpd is the server every OpenWrt image has. It does TLS, keep-alive and the socket work; the exporter never listens on anything itself.
  • The library. /usr/share/ucode/prometheus/exporter/ holds the modules that the handler, the command line, check and the ubus object share, prometheus.exporter.<module>: the loader, the configuration, the scrape, the exposition format, the jail's rules. In front of them, /usr/share/ucode/prometheus/exporter.uc is the collector API, prometheus.exporter.
  • The collectors. One module each, in /usr/share/ucode/prometheus/collectors/, installed by the base package or by a package of its own.
  • The ubus object. rpcd serves prometheus-exporter from a ucode plugin. It is how LuCI, or a script, asks the exporter what it would do: which collectors are installed, whether a value is valid, how each collector does.
  • The init script. It checks the configuration and works out the jail from what the collectors declare. It grants the jail's user what the collectors need (its ubus ACL, capabilities, groups, read access). Then it hands procd the uhttpd instance, which runs as that user, never as root.

docs.title: A process per request
docs.text:
uhttpd-mod-ucode runs the handler once, when uhttpd starts, and then answers each request in a process forked from that one. So everything the handler did at load time is already done in every request: the collectors are compiled and validated once, and the configuration's compress and basic auth are read once. And nothing a request does is there for the next: its memory goes with its process.

That shapes two choices.

First, loading is the place for anything costly that does not change between scrapes, and a change to what was loaded needs a restart, not a reload. Installing a collector package reloads the service. The init script has procd watch every collector module and config the jail mounts, and procd restarts uhttpd when one changed.

Second, what must outlast a request has to go to disk. Two things must:

  • Basic auth's cache. Checking a password against its hash costs a scrape a large share of its time on a slow CPU, and a cache in memory would be gone by the next request.
  • The ledger: how long each collector takes, and its circuit breaker. These order the next scrape and say what its deadline has time for (see About deadlines and circuit breakers).

So each uhttpd instance has a small state directory on tmpfs, the one path its jail mounts read-write, and its files are named after the instance. The handler names its instance when uhttpd loads it, by the pid and start time of that process, which no later process can share, and it removes every other instance's files then. A restart starts without state. That is what a changed password or a changed collector should mean anyway, and it is how a quarantined collector is tried again at once.

Requests run at once, so the state is written under a lock: an exclusive flock() of the instance's lock file, which the kernel lets go of however a request ends. Each write is a whole new file renamed over the old one, so a read, which takes no lock, never sees half a file. And a scrape records itself by reading the ledger again under the lock and adding to it, so scrapes that ran at once each count.

docs.title: A process of its own
docs.text:
A scrape cannot trust its collectors to return. One may loop forever, wait on a FIFO that nothing writes to, allocate until the memory runs out, or call exit(). Within one process there is no stopping that. ucode's VM runs a signal handler at its next instruction, which would do, but uhttpd-mod-ucode's VM handles no signals at all (a handler is never called, and the signal's default action ends the request). And a native call blocked in a system call would not reach the next instruction anyway.

So each scrape forks a child, with ucode's uloop.task, from the process that already has the collectors loaded: a fork costs no compiling. The child goes through the scrape's plan itself, forked with it. It runs the collectors one after the other, the fastest first, and leaves out those that the deadline, a breaker or the reply's sample limit keeps out, as the scrape would. The scrape holds a timer on the collector that runs. When the collector's budget ends, or the scrape's deadline comes first, the scrape:

  • kills the child, with every process under it (a program the collector started would otherwise run on, its parent gone);
  • records the collector as stopped;
  • forks another child, which goes on after it.

A child that dies under a collector, out of memory or from a crash, costs that collector alone. Each process of the service has a data limit, so a collector that allocates without end aborts its own child, not the router.

The limit the scrape holds a collector to is the child's word, and the child is where the collectors run. A collector that by mistake writes over the plan the child keeps could have the child give a limit past the deadline, or none, or start collectors the deadline leaves no time for. So the scrape also holds the child to the scrape's deadline, whatever the child says:

  • A collector the child runs is stopped at the deadline at the latest.
  • A child that runs past the deadline with no collector started is stopped a turn of the timer later, a tenth of a second.

The scrape then forks no other child. It goes through the rest of the plan itself, in its own process, where no collector ran, and leaves out every collector left at the deadline (SCRAPE_DEADLINE). The runs the child finished before are served. A child that keeps to its limits never meets this: its collectors end at the deadline at the latest, and it hands back the collectors it leaves out at once.

What the child does crosses back to the scrape through a file. The scrape made the file for the child before forking it, and removed it as soon as it was made. Before each collector, the child writes a line saying that it started, with its limit. After the collector, it writes its run: its samples as the text the reply will hold, never re-encoded. A run and the next collector's line go in one write. The scrape reads the file through a descriptor of its own while the child goes on, at its timer's turns and when the child tells it to. So on a router with two cores, the scrape takes in the runs while the child runs the next collector. It holds its timer on the collector the last line names.

The pipe between them carries only short messages:

  • that the child started a collector whose limit is near, which the scrape could be past before its timer's next turn;
  • that the child has runs worth taking at once;
  • that the child has ended.

They are short enough that the scrape reads them whole: ucode's uloop reads the pipe without blocking, and loses a message that is half there.

sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Prometheus
    participant S as The scrape, the request's process
    participant C as The child, forked with the plan
    participant F as The runs file
    P->>S: GET /metrics, with its timeout
    S->>C: fork
    loop each collector, fastest first
        C->>F: the last run, and the line that this one starts, with its limit
        C-->>S: pipe, when a limit is near or runs are worth taking
        S->>F: read, at the timer's turns
    end
    alt a collector runs past its budget
        S->>C: kill, with every process under it
        S->>C: fork another child, which goes on after it
    else the deadline comes
        S->>C: kill, with every process under it
        Note over S: leaves out every collector left, SCRAPE_DEADLINE
    end
    C-->>S: pipe, the child's end
    S->>P: the reply, with the runs it has

A run belongs to the collector it names, never to the one the scrape holds its timer on. Stopping a child takes a few milliseconds, since the processes under it must be found and killed. A collector that ends in those milliseconds, past its limit, has its run and the next collector's start written before the child dies. That collector keeps its run, and the next one, which the child had started, runs again in the child forked after it.

The child keeps a progress file beside the ledger, named by the scrape's process: a line before each collector, with the child it runs in. If the scrape process itself dies, killed from outside, the next scrape finds the file, names the collector that was running, quarantines it, and kills the child it may have left looping.

Loading is guarded the same way. uhttpd loads the collectors once, in the process every scrape is forked from, so a module whose top level never returns would keep uhttpd from ever serving. So each module is first checked in a child, for five seconds at most: its text, and then its exports, as the loader checks them.

Five seconds stop a loop. They do not stop a call that ends the process or writes to it, nor one that does what the child would survive and uhttpd would not. And what a top level does in the child it may do again in uhttpd, where nothing stops it. So a top level only declares. At both loads, while it runs, the functions of ucode that block, end or write to the process, load code or change its signals refuse to run, and the module is left out (see The top level).

Only the modules that passed there are loaded for real, all of them as one program, each only when its meta is the one checked. What they share, the collector API and the modules behind it, is then compiled once. A program for each collector would compile it once per collector, and keep each copy's source files open. The loader itself is compiled in that child, and never in uhttpd, which holds what it loads for as long as it runs (see Performance on small routers).

rpcd must never hang either, since it serves the whole of LuCI. So it asks a helper process to load a module it has not seen before, once per version of the module.

This costs a scrape a fork, a line and a run in the file for each collector, plus the file itself; see Performance on small routers.

When no child can be forked (the system is out of processes or memory), or the file the runs cross by cannot be made, the scrape runs the rest of its collectors in its own process, unguarded, rather than not at all.

docs.title: Only one module touches the system
docs.text:
prometheus.exporter.deps and its modules, one per capability (deps/ubus.uc, deps/exec.uc, ...), are the only ones that import fs, ubus, uci, rtnl, nl80211 and socket. A collector does not import them. It declares in meta.needs the capabilities it wants, and collect receives exactly those, in its deps argument. All it takes of the exporter's code comes from one module, prometheus.exporter, the collector API, and it imports no other: the loader refuses one that does, before loading it. The API is to collectors what the ubus object and the configuration are to scripts: the surface a version promises. Behind it, the core's modules move freely.

This is dependency injection, and it pays three times:

  • Tests. A test builds deps from utest's mocks, fed with what real devices answered, and runs the collector as a scrape would. No collector needs a router to be tested.
  • The jail. What a collector may reach is written down, so the service can build the jail from it, rather than from a list someone keeps by hand.
  • The narrowing. deps is not the module, but a channel over it that hands out less: fs without its writing functions; uci as handles on the configs a collector named and nothing else, read-only and of the committed configuration only; exec only for the programs listed, and with a deadline. A collector that tries for more has no way to get it.

Taking every native function by name in one module also makes make lint meaningful. Loading that module on OpenWrt 25.12's ucode fails if the release lacks a function the exporter uses, at build time and not in a scrape.

docs.title: The loader
docs.text:
The loader takes every module of the collectors' directory and:

  1. refuses one that is not in strict mode (in strict mode a variable never declared is an error, not a global every later collector sees), or that imports anything but the collector API;
  2. loads each in a child process first;
  3. loads those that loaded there as one program;
  4. validates each one's meta and collect;
  5. leaves out one that does not load in time or is not valid, logging why.

The handler has it do all of that in the child, and keeps what passed there. Should the one program not load, each module is loaded alone, as it was in its child.

Loaded together, the collectors share the API's modules, as they share the child they run in. What the API exports (Result, errors, services, proc, exposition) are functions and constants, to call and to read. A collector that wrote over one would write over it for the others too, and strict mode does not stop that. So each is a module's namespace, which ucode keeps constant, and so is a Result's prototype: writing over one fails. And what a top level writes to the global scope would stay in uhttpd for every scrape. So the loader puts the global scope back as it was once a top level has run, and leaves out a module that changed it. The exporter guards against mistakes, not against code written to get round it (see Buggy, not hostile).

What a collector is handed is its own. Each run gets a deps made for it, and each capability with it, so a collector that writes over deps.fs.readfile changes it for itself alone. A broken subpackage costs its own collector and nothing else. The same loader runs in the handler, the command line, check, the jail's script and the ubus object, so all of them agree on what is installed.

While the probe waits for its child, uloop takes SIGTERM and SIGINT, and uhttpd's own loop, which starts after the handler, would never see them. procd's SIGTERM to an instance still loading its collectors, as in an upgrade of several packages, would then leave it serving without them until procd killed it. So each module not yet loaded is reported stopped, and the handler ends, as the signal would have ended it.

A scrape waits for its collectors' child in a loop of uloop's too, and so do check, the ubus object's status and the command line's scrape. SIGTERM or SIGINT (procd stopping a request, or Ctrl-C at a terminal) ends the wait. The scrape then:

  • kills the child, with every process under it;
  • keeps the runs that ended, and takes none of the rest for a collector's failure;
  • removes its progress file, so that the next scrape blames no collector for it;
  • ends, as the signal would have ended it.

docs.title: Why the ubus object lives in rpcd
docs.text:
The handler only runs inside a request, and only in the jail. Something has to answer questions about the exporter when nobody scrapes, outside the jail, and to LuCI. That is rpcd, which every image runs, and which already serves LuCI's other objects. Its plugin reads with the exporter's own modules, so it sees what the exporter sees.

One method, status, runs a scrape. Collectors call ubus objects, and some of those objects are rpcd's own (wireguard, luci), which rpcd cannot answer while it waits for the scrape. So status runs the scrape in a process of its own and replies when that process is done; rpcd answers other calls meanwhile. That process runs the collectors in the service's own jail, with ujail, as check and the command line's scrape do, so all of them find what Prometheus gets. And rpcd kills it, with all it started, if it ever outlives a scrape's time.

docs.title: About Deadlines and Circuit Breakers
docs.text: A scrape that answers late is worth nothing: Prometheus drops all of it, not only the part that was slow. And a collector that hangs, or fails every time, costs every scrape. This page covers how the exporter keeps a scrape on time, why it sets a misbehaving collector aside for a while, and what that costs.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Prometheus waits scrape_timeout, 10 seconds unless a job says otherwise, and then gives up on the scrape. It does not keep what came in time: up is 0, and every series of the target has a gap. On a fast router that never happens. On a 500-MIPS MIPS router, nat_traffic alone takes 8 to 9 seconds on a table of 20,000 connections. One busy evening, and every metric of the router goes dark, its load, its memory and its interfaces with it.

The same is true of a program that hangs. ubnt-manager logging in to a radio that does not answer holds its collector for its whole timeout, 5 seconds, every scrape.

docs.title: A deadline per scrape
docs.text:
So each scrape has a deadline. Prometheus says how long it waits, in X-Prometheus-Scrape-Timeout-Seconds, and so does vmagent. A scraper that does not say gets the main section's scrape_timeout, 10 seconds by default, as is both scrapers' own default. Neither may be more than uhttpd gives the handler, 60 seconds (its -t), after which uhttpd kills the request and answers nothing.

The collectors get all of it but half a second. That half second is for the network and the scraper, as blackbox_exporter's own --timeout-offset keeps by default. Writing the reply is reckoned apart, because it grows with the samples: 52 ms for 33,000 of them in the devenv (the development container, on a laptop), some thirty times that on a slow router. The exporter measures it per sample as it goes, and keeps back what the samples so far, and the next collector's, will take.

The deadline is checked before each collector, and a collector is started only if what it took before still fits:

  • One that does not fit is left out, with node_scrape_collector_success 0 and the error SCRAPE_DEADLINE.
  • One that is running when the deadline comes is stopped there, with the process it runs in (see About the architecture), and fails with SCRAPE_DEADLINE too.

The scrape enforces the deadline itself, whatever that process says. The process goes through the plan and tells the scrape each collector's limit, but a collector that went wrong there could make it give a later limit, or none. The scrape stops it at the deadline all the same, and leaves out every collector it had not run.

A program never runs past the deadline. When the whole seconds left before the deadline are fewer than the program's own, it gets those, and it is killed with everything it started when they are spent. The watchdog counts whole seconds, so a program is not started with less than one left.

The scrape logs the collectors it left out in one line, not one each. On a router whose table is always large, that line is the same every scrape, and a line per collector would only repeat it.

docs.title: Fastest first
docs.text:
Checking between collectors is only as good as the order they run in. In the order of their names, a slow collector in the middle takes every collector after it down with it. So each uhttpd instance keeps a ledger of how long each collector took, and runs them fastest first. When time runs short, it is the slow one, at the end, that is left out, and the many fast ones are served.

A collector never timed runs after those the ledger knows, since it may be the slow one. Among those never timed, the exporter's own run before those of other packages, and one that declares itself heavy (meta.cost) runs after the rest of its kind. The declaration orders and does nothing else. The deadline leaves a collector out only by what the ledger measured, so one that calls itself heavy is still run, and timed. The reply is in the same order whatever the run order: the collectors as the query names them, or by name.

A collector's estimate is a moving average that weighs the last run by 0.25. A collector takes much the same time scrape after scrape, but some things grow or shrink, such as the conntrack table. At 0.25, a one-scrape spike is half gone two scrapes later, and a lasting change is nine tenths there after eight. Before an instance has measured writing a reply, it reckons 50 µs a sample, a 500-MIPS MIPS core's, so a reply is never reckoned shorter than on the slowest router.

docs.title: Circuit breakers
docs.text:
A deadline protects one scrape. A collector that hangs, or fails every time, needs more: it should stop costing scrapes at all, for a while. That is a circuit breaker, one per collector.

A breaker trips when the collector:

  • has a program killed at its own timeout, since it would be again;
  • is still running at the end of its budget, collector_budget (5 seconds, half of Prometheus's default timeout) unless its section sets budget. It is stopped there, with the process it runs in, and fails with COLLECTOR_CANCELLED;
  • ends the process it runs in, out of memory, by a crash or by exit() (COLLECTOR_KILLED), or is running when its scrape process dies;
  • fails three scrapes in a row. One failure is often a passing one, a service restarting or a reload; three are 45 seconds of failures at a 15-second interval.

Nothing to observe never counts: it is a success. A collector the deadline left out has neither succeeded nor failed.

A tripped breaker quarantines its collector: it is not run for 1 scrape, then 2, 4, 8, 16, and at most 32. The scrape after that is its trial. A trial that succeeds closes the breaker; one that fails in any way doubles the cool-down. While it is quarantined, the collector answers node_scrape_collector_success 0 and ucode_prometheus_exporter_collector_quarantined 1. The log has one line when the breaker trips and one when it closes, and nothing between.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Closed
    Closed --> Closed: succeeds, or fails fewer than three times in a row
    Closed --> Quarantined: trips
    Quarantined --> Trial: cool-down spent, 1, 2, 4 ... 32 scrapes
    Trial --> Closed: succeeds
    Trial --> Quarantined: fails in any way, cool-down doubled

The cap is a trade-off. A broken collector costs at most one trial every 32 scrapes, and a trial is bounded by its budget and the scrape's deadline. A fixed one waits at most 32 scrapes to be served again: 8 minutes at Prometheus's usual 15 seconds, 32 at vmagent's minute. A shorter cap would serve fixed collectors sooner and cost more trials; a longer one the reverse.

A collector that runs programs gets a budget of at least its timeout and a second more, since the watchdog counts whole seconds. So a budget never quarantines what a timeout allows.

docs.title: Counted in scrapes, kept per instance
docs.text:
Cool-downs are counted in the instance's scrapes, not in seconds. A router scraped every minute and one scraped every 10 seconds both try a collector again after the same share of their scrapes. Every scrape of the instance counts, whoever makes it and whatever it selects.

The exporter has no long-lived process of its own to remember anything in. uhttpd answers each request in a process forked from the one that loaded the handler, and that process is gone once it answers. So the ledger, durations and breakers both, is a file in the instance's state directory, on tmpfs, read when a scrape starts and written when it ends. Scrapes can run at once: a scraper, LuCI and someone with curl. Each writes under the state's lock, re-reading the ledger as it is then and adding what it saw, so none is lost and no reader sees half a file.

The ledger is the instance's, and the service's restart starts a new instance without it: every duration and every breaker is forgotten. That is how to try a quarantined collector now, rather than at its trial. A reload that procd does not turn into a restart keeps the ledger.

docs.title: Quarantine applies to every scrape
docs.text:
A scrape that names a quarantined collector in collect[] does not run it either. The alternative, running whatever is asked for, would let any job that names the collector pay its cost every scrape, and trip and re-trip its breaker. The way to scrape a slow collector is a job of its own, with a longer timeout. With its budget raised to match, it is not quarantined in the first place.

While the exporter collector, in the base package, is selected, the scrape counts what happened since the service started, by collector: ucode_prometheus_exporter_quarantines_total, _deadline_skips_total, _program_timeouts_total and _collector_failures_total. So an alert can ask how often, not only whether now. The counters live in the same ledger, and a restart starts them again at 0, as a new process's counters would.

The scrape writes these counters itself, once its collectors have run, as it writes node_scrape_collector_*. The collector does not write them, because the deadline would leave it out first, in the very scrapes the deadline skips count. So they are in every scrape, this one's skips included, whatever the deadline, a breaker or a crash did to the collectors, the exporter collector among them.

check and LuCI's status page are different. They run a scrape of their own, in the service's jail, to show what each collector does now, quarantined or not. Beside it, they show what the service's own scrapes found, from the running instance's ledger: each collector quarantined, why, and when it is tried again, and each the deadline left out lately.

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text:
• The first scrape after a restart can still be late. The ledger is empty then. The exporter's own collectors run first, those that declare themselves heavy (nat_traffic, ethtool) after the others, then those of other packages, and a slow one can still take the deadline with the rest. The second scrape knows. Nothing of the ledger survives a restart, by design: a restart is how to forget a quarantine.
  • A collector too slow for the timeout is left out for a while. The ledger says it does not fit, so it is not run, and not timed. Each scrape that leaves it out makes its estimate three quarters of itself, so that it is tried again, and timed, after a few (3 when it was twice too slow, 9 when ten times). So one slow run costs a few scrapes, not the instance's life. One that is always too slow is tried, and stopped at the deadline, once in a few scrapes. A job with a longer timeout runs it, and keeps its estimate current.
  • Two scrapes at once can each run a trial. Each sees the cool-down over, and each counts its trial: two that fail double the cool-down twice.
  • A program needs a whole second before the deadline. A collector whose program would take 10 ms is left out when less than a second is left. Since the fastest run first, the collectors with programs run early, while time is plentiful.
