docs.title: About the Security Model
docs.text: The exporter runs on a router, as a user of its own, and answers requests from the network. It reads much of what the router knows: its interfaces and addresses, its clients and leases, its configuration. This page covers what keeps that access to reading, and the trade-offs made along the way.

docs.title: A jail built from declarations
docs.text:
uhttpd, and the exporter in it, runs in procd's jail. The jail holds:

  • the exporter's own code and libraries, procfs, sysfs and the log;
  • what the installed and enabled collectors declare: the configs they read, the programs they run, the files and directories they read, and the ubus socket while one of them needs ubus.

Nothing else of /etc/config is there, and nothing is writable but the exporter's small state directory.

The jail is computed, not written by hand. Each collector's meta says what it needs. The init script asks jail.uc what that adds up to, and procd mounts the result. A collector the device does not install, or that its configuration disables, adds nothing. This is what keeps the jail tight: it is exactly as wide as the collectors in use, and it stays right as packages come and go, without anyone keeping a list.

flowchart TD
    M[the enabled collectors' meta] --> I[init script and jail.uc, as root]
    subgraph jail[procd's jail, as the user prometheus-exporter]
        U[uhttpd and the handler] --> C[collectors]
    end
    I -- "mounts, ubus ACL, capabilities, groups, read access" --> jail
    C -- "only the calls the ACL allows" --> B[ubusd]
    B --> D[netifd, hostapd, dnsmasq and other daemons]
    B --> O[the prometheus-exporter object, in rpcd as root]
    O -- "reads with uci" --> K[(configs that hold keys)]

The service's ubus object reads what the jail may not, and hands back only the fields a collector reads (see Not root).

Some declarations are refused outright:

  • a path that is not absolute, or not plain;
  • directories that hold what every service has: /etc/config, /run, /tmp, /usr/lib and the like.

A collector cannot ask for a socket in /run, because the jail would then hold every service's sockets. ujail cannot mount a socket by itself, so a collector names the socket's directory instead, and that directory must be its service's alone, as Unbound's /var/lib/unbound is.

A directory the exporter owns, textfile's, is held tighter, because the service makes it as root and mounts it. It must be under /var, /tmp or /etc/prometheus-exporter, and not under /var/run or /tmp/run, where every service, the exporter included, keeps its sockets and secrets. A value elsewhere is refused before anything is made. This is an allowlist, not the list of shared directories above: whoever may write the exporter's configuration, such as a LuCI login allowed this app alone, cannot have the service make directories in, or mount, the rest of the filesystem.

And /tmp is everyone's. On OpenWrt /var is a link to it, and any user may make a directory there. A user that starts before the service could make textfile's /var/prometheus its own, and feed the exporter metrics. Or it could make it a link to a directory it chose, which root would then make directories under and mount. So the service walks the path from / before it makes or mounts it:

  • each directory must be root's, and writable by no one else unless it is sticky, as /tmp is;
  • a link must be root's alone, as /var is;
  • what is not there, the service makes, root's and 0755, and then checks what it made.

A path that fails is neither made nor mounted, and the service logs why.

That makes /tmp safe to allow, and it stays allowed: its directories are on tmpfs, so a script that writes there every minute does not wear the flash. /var, which the default is under, is /tmp. Another user can still make the directory first, and so keep textfile from reading it until root removes it: a nuisance the service logs, not a way in. For a directory no other user can touch, use one under /etc/prometheus-exporter.

The ubus socket matters most of these. ubusd lets root call every object, so a jail running as root with the socket could ask rpcd, netifd or any service for anything they answer. Mounts limit what the exporter can see, not what it can do over ubus. So the jail has the socket only while a collector that needs ubus is enabled, and it does not run as root: ubusd holds it to an ACL of the calls the enabled collectors declare (see Not root).

The jail has the host's network, not one of its own, because uhttpd must answer on the router's addresses. So a collector that reads a service over TCP, as agh reads AdGuard Home's HTTP API, needs no mount; the capability is what bounds it. deps.socket.tcp_request connects only to an address of the device itself. It binds to that address first, so an address that is not the router's fails before anything is sent. A collector's address is an option, set by whoever may write the exporter's configuration, a LuCI login allowed this app alone among them. Bounded this way, it can point the exporter at a port of the router, never at a host of the LAN or beyond. And the collector reads only what answers without a login: agh sends no credentials, since a password the jail's user could read would be a secret in the jail.

The jail is a boundary for the exporter's own mistakes as much as for an attacker's. A collector that parses something wrong cannot write anywhere, and one whose program hangs is killed with everything it started.

Read-only is not the same as harmless, so some files stay out of the jail even when a collector needs part of what they hold. /etc/config/network holds WireGuard's private keys, and the wireguard collector does not declare it. To name peers by their descriptions (peer_names), it asks the service's ubus object, which reads the config as root and hands over only each peer's public key and description. The keys stay out of the jail's files, and out of every reply the service's user may ask for (see What the service's user reaches over ubus). The ubus object's interfaces, by contrast, asks netifd, so that a LuCI user allowed only the exporter's object gets interface names without the file.

docs.title: Not root
docs.text:
uhttpd runs in its jail as the user and group prometheus-exporter, which the package makes, with no new privileges. Not being root is what gives the rest of the jail its meaning. Root reads every file whatever its mode, may call every ubus object, and has every capability: for root, the jail's mounts would be all that stood between a mistake and the router. As the service's user, the process reads what the files' modes let it, ubusd refuses it what the ACL does not allow, and it has no capability at all unless an enabled collector declares one.

What a collector needs beyond that, it declares, as it declares its mounts:

  • its ubus calls;
  • its capabilities;
  • the groups whose sockets it connects to;
  • read access, for the service's group, to the root-only files of /proc and the configs it reads.

The service grants these as root, at each start, and only while the collector is enabled. It takes back what no enabled collector declares any more, a disabled or a removed collector's, and gives each file back the group and mode it had. It takes back all of it when the service stops, is disabled or is removed. So the privileges are as wide as the collectors in use, and stay right as collectors come and go, as the mounts do. See The jail for each.

This took some choices:

  • The ubus ACL is written for the enabled collectors, not installed for all of them. An ACL that each package installed would allow its calls as long as the package is there, enabled or not. So the service writes the ACL at each start, for the collectors enabled then, with the options they have, and has ubusd read it again. It keeps the ACL outside its run directory, which only root enters, and a link in ubusd's directory, which the package installs, points to it.

  • No call that answers a secret, or reads what its caller names. ubusd's ACL names objects and methods, never their arguments, so a method is as wide as the widest reply it gives. Some methods a collector would reach for answer more than it reads:

    • rpcd's file read reads any file as root, and checks no session for a caller that sends none;
    • its uci get reads any config;
    • netifd's network.wireless status holds every Wi-Fi network's key;
    • procd's service list holds every service's command line and environment.

    The ACL allows none of them. Where a collector needs a little of what they answer, the service's own ubus object, which rpcd runs as root, asks for it and hands over the fields the collector reads, and nothing else. Its methods for the collectors take no arguments, so no caller can point them elsewhere.

  • The object's methods for the collectors never hold rpcd on another daemon. rpcd serves every object of its plugins in one process, one call at a time, LuCI's and the collectors' rc list and wireguard status among them. A call that waited on a daemon would hold them all. So wireless and wireguard_peers ask no daemon. They read the committed wireless and network configs with uci, and the phys in sysfs, in rpcd's own process, and keep only the fields above, by name. An option they do not name, such as a key, a password, a secret or one not there yet, never leaves rpcd. wireless keeps its last reply, which holds no more than it answered, to give again while the configs' files and the phys are as they were.

    netifd is not asked. It held the keys in its network.wireless status, and it can be busy for seconds while it sets a radio up. What only netifd knew, which interfaces are there and up, the collector asks the kernel itself, over nl80211 and in sysfs, which the jail already had for it (see ubus object for how the config's networks are named as netifd names them).

    time_daemons must ask procd. The jail has a PID namespace of its own, so its /proc lists the jail's processes, not ntpd's or chronyd's. And rpcd's rc list, which the jail may call, says whether a service runs by forking each init script's running. So time_daemons asks procd's service list without waiting for the answer, over a connection with a timeout of 3 s, and replies when procd answers; rpcd answers other calls meanwhile. None of these methods runs a program.

  • Capabilities that read, never ones that read past the jail. A collector may declare CAP_NET_ADMIN or CAP_NET_RAW. Reading /proc/net/nf_conntrack, which is root's alone, would be easiest with CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH. But that capability opens any file of a filesystem the jail has a file of, by its handle, past every mount. And CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE would write the jail's procfs. So the service gives that one file to its group instead, as it does the configs.

  • Configs opened to the group, secrets copied. OpenWrt's configs are mostly root's alone (0600), and a collector reads its configs where uci keeps them. So the service gives the configs the jail mounts to its group, read-only, and takes them back once no enabled collector reads them. uci commit gives a config back to root's group, and the reload it triggers gives it to the service's group again. Secrets are handled differently. Basic auth's file is written for the group at each start. The TLS certificate and key are read from copies the service makes at each start and removes when it stops. So /etc/uhttpd.key and the hash's config stay root's alone.

  • Root copies a TLS file from where certificates are kept, and nowhere else. A copy is root reading a file the configuration names, and handing it to the service's group. Whoever may write the configuration, such as a LuCI login allowed this app alone, could otherwise have root copy /etc/shadow into the jail, or read /dev/zero until the router runs out of memory. So cert and key are taken only:

    • under /etc/ssl (certificates, and OpenWrt's acme's), /etc/acme (acme.sh's) and /etc/prometheus-exporter (the exporter's own);
    • as /etc/uhttpd.* (uhttpd's own, which LuCI serves with).

    Those hold certificates and keys and nothing of the system's, and only root writes them. The rest of /etc, which holds the system's secrets, is not allowed. The file must also be a regular file of at most 64 KiB, a chain of certificates' size, and its links, if any, must leave it in those places. A configuration that breaks this is refused with TLS_PATH or TLS_FILE wherever it is checked: LuCI, validate, check, start and reload alike. jail.uc --make checks again before it reads at most that much, and the init script serves HTTPS only from the copies it made.

  • A capability is the whole process's. The scrape's child processes are uhttpd's. So while nft-counters is enabled, CAP_NET_ADMIN is uhttpd's too, and uhttpd is the process that answers requests from the network. What it can change of the network is what that capability allows. A router that does not need nft's counters does not enable the collector.

What stays root's is what must:

  • the init script and jail.uc, which grant;
  • rpcd's ubus object, which writes the hash;
  • the watch instance, which asks procd for a reload by an event. Otherwise the service's ACL would have to allow that call, for any event.

docs.title: What the service's user reaches over ubus
docs.text:
These are all the calls the ACL can allow. Each is allowed only while a collector that declares it is enabled (check lists the ACL in force). None takes an argument that chooses what is read, and none answers a key, a password or a hash.

Call Declared by What it answers system board Every ACL (the canary), openwrt The board's model and OpenWrt's release. rc list agh, bmx7, chrony, dawn, dhcp_leases, dnsmasq, modemmanager, mwan3, timesync, unbound Each init script's start and stop priorities, and whether it is enabled and running. network.interface dump dhcp_leases, openwrt_interfaces netifd's status of each logical interface: its addresses, routes, DNS servers and uptime; not its config. prometheus-exporter wireless wifi, hostapd_stations Each radio's name, disabled, channel, country and HT mode, and each of its networks' interface, SSID or mesh ID, and encryption; not the wireless config, which has the keys. prometheus-exporter time_daemons timesync Whether busybox ntpd and chronyd run: two booleans, not procd's command lines. prometheus-exporter wireguard_peers wireguard with peer_names Each WireGuard peer's public key and description, by interface; not the peer sections, which hold the preshared keys. prometheus-exporter.filesystem mounts filesystem Each of the host's mounts with blocks: its device, mount point, type, read-only flag, sizes and inodes. wireguard status wireguard rpcd-mod-wireguard's interfaces and peers: public keys, listen ports, endpoints, allowed IPs, traffic and last handshakes; no private or preshared key. hostapd.<interface> get_status, get_clients hostapd_stations; hostapd_ubus_stations (get_clients) Each access point's SSID, BSSID, channel and airtime, and its stations: MAC addresses, flags, rates, signal and traffic. dhcp ipv4leases, ipv6leases dhcp_leases odhcpd's leases: addresses, MAC addresses, DUIDs and host names. dnsmasq metrics dnsmasq dnsmasq's counters. dawn get_network dawn DAWN's access points and clients. mwan3 status mwan3 mwan3's interfaces and their tracking. poe info realtek-poe The PoE ports' state and power. dsl metrics ltq-dsl The DSL line's state and counters.

A collector of another package may declare calls of its own, which the ACL then allows while it is enabled. Installing it is trusting it with them, as with its code (see Buggy, not hostile). The leases, stations and clients are what a router knows of the people on its network, and they are what those collectors are for. Leave the collectors disabled where their series should not leave the router.

docs.title: Buggy, not hostile
docs.text:
Collectors come from packages: the exporter's own, and others that anyone may write. Most of what can go wrong with a collector is a bug:

  • a loop whose condition never turns false;
  • a read of a FIFO that nothing writes to;
  • a table that grows past what anyone expected;
  • a family named like another collector's;
  • an allocation that never stops.

The exporter is built so that such a collector costs only itself. It runs in a process of its own, is stopped at its budget, is limited in samples and memory, is kept to its own families, and is quarantined when it keeps failing. The collector contract lists every rule and what breaking it costs.

What the exporter does not do, and cannot, is contain a hostile collector. A collector is code that a root package installed. It runs in the exporter's own process, as the service's user, with every privilege the enabled collectors were granted, its own or not. Its module is loaded where the handler is. It can call whatever ucode and the modules it imports can, and it could undo any limit set from inside that process. Containing hostile code takes a boundary it cannot reach from where it runs, a user and a kernel sandbox around each collector, and that is a different design with a different cost. Here the boundary is installing the package: a collector package is code you choose to run, installed by root like any other package. What the service's user bounds is what all the collectors together may do.

So the guards are written against mistakes. They hold a collector to what it declared and to what a scrape can afford. They make its failure visible: a reply that says so, a log line, a counter, a quarantine. And they keep the rest of the scrape on time. They do not try to outwit code that means to escape them.

docs.title: What collectors get
docs.text:
Inside the jail, a collector gets less than the jail holds. It receives capabilities, not modules:

  • the fs functions that read, and none that write;
  • uci handles on the configs it named, read-only and of the committed configuration only, so a change staged in uci but not committed is never read;
  • programs from its own list only, run without a shell interpreting their arguments, and killed with their children when its seconds are spent.

See About the architecture.

And a collector imports one module only, the collector API, so it has no way to the system but those capabilities. A collector that imports fs, or calls require('fs'), is refused before it is loaded. This too is a rule against mistakes. An author used to ucode scripts imports fs without a second thought, and a collector ported from elsewhere reaches for the module it knew. The loader reads the module's text for its imports and those calls, which is what such a collector has. Code written to get round the rule, reaching require some other way, would get round it, and would be hostile.

The tests hold our collectors to what they declare in the same spirit. They run each collector in the filesystem its jail gives it, so a read of a path it did not declare fails the test, rather than passing there and finding nothing in the service.

docs.title: Basic auth, over TLS only
docs.text:
Basic auth sends the password with every request, encoded but not encrypted. Over HTTP, anyone on the path reads it. So the exporter takes basic auth over HTTPS only. auth_user and auth_password without cert and key are an invalid configuration, refused wherever it is checked: start, reload, check, the ubus object's validate and LuCI alike. A configuration that asks for a login is never served without TLS, not even with a warning.

auth_password holds a crypt hash, never the password, so the configuration, its backups and LuCI's forms never hold the secret. The ubus object makes the hash, so the password is not on a command line, where ps would show it. Neither the password nor the hash is logged, and no reply of the ubus object holds the hash.

The hash is also kept apart, in /etc/config/prometheus-exporter-auth, mode 0600, not in the exporter's config. LuCI's ACL for the app grants reading the exporter's config, which a login that may only look at the settings needs. Were the hash there, that login could read it through rpcd's uci object, and guess the password offline at a hash's pace. So the app's ACL grants nothing of the hash's config, to read or to write. LuCI asks the ubus object's password whether one is saved, and hands a new password to set_password, which hashes it as root, saves the hash and reloads the service.

So the password is changed at once, apart from Save & Apply, as LuCI's own router password is, and the page says so. A change LuCI staged in the login's session could not be seen there, since the session lists only the changes of configs it may read: its Unsaved Changes would leave the hash out, and its Revert would leave it staged. The jail does not mount that config either. The handler reads uhttpd's file instead, a copy the service writes when it starts, which the service's group reads.

docs.title: Why the handler checks the password itself
docs.text:
uhttpd has basic auth of its own: a config file of prefix:user:hash lines (-c), with a realm (-r). The init script writes that file, and uhttpd reads it. But OpenWrt 25.12's uhttpd applies it to files and CGI only, not to a handler's prefix, so a request to /metrics would reach the handler without a login. uhttpd fixed this in August 2026 (commit 3aa7e1c), after every 25.12 release so far.

So the handler reads the same file when it starts, and checks every request against it before it scrapes, computing the hash in ucode as musl's crypt would. On a uhttpd that does check, the request is checked twice. On one that does not, it is checked once, which is what matters.

The handler fails closed. A file that is there but wrong denies every request. So does a missing file while the configuration sets auth_user. If the file goes and procd starts uhttpd again as it was, with no file for the jail to mount, the handler reads the exporter's configuration, which the jail has, and denies every request rather than serve without the login it asks for.

The hash is computed for any user, so a wrong user takes as long as a wrong password.

docs.title: The cache, and what it trades
docs.text:
Computing a hash costs real time on a router's CPU: 135 ms for hash_password's 1000 rounds of SHA-512-crypt on a 500-MIPS MIPS core, at every scrape. And uhttpd's process per request keeps nothing in memory. So after it lets a request in, the handler writes the SHA-256 of that request's exact Authorization header to its state directory, bound to the user and the hash. A later request with the same header is let in on that digest, compared in constant time. Any other header pays the full check, and a wrong one stays out and leaves the entry as it was. A changed user or password lets nothing in by the old entry, and a restart forgets it.

The digest reveals no more than what is already on the device. It sits beside the hash, as closed: the service's user's alone, in its state directory of mode 0700 on tmpfs, inside a directory only root enters, never on flash or in a backup. Finding a header that gives the digest is guessing the password, as with the hash, only cheaper per guess: one SHA-256 against a thousand rounds and more. That matters only to whoever can read the file: root on the router, or the service itself. Either can also read the password from the next scrape, since uhttpd ends the TLS. A long random password, as a scraper's should be, is out of reach either way.

docs.title: Why the rounds are capped
docs.text: A $5$ or $6$ hash may name up to 9,999,999 rounds. A hash of that many would take a 500-MIPS router twenty minutes per scrape, so anyone who can set the configuration could make the exporter burn the router's CPU. So a hash may have at most 2000 rounds, a quarter of a second there. A hash that names none, which means 5000, is refused like any invalid value. See Performance on small routers.

docs.title: Defaults that face inward
docs.text:
The exporter listens on loopback until told otherwise, so a fresh install exposes nothing. listen_interface takes a logical interface, so the exporter follows that interface's addresses. *, every address, is a choice to make deliberately, since it includes the WAN's.

Once the exporter listens on the LAN, the port is meant for the scrapers alone, and the firewall is what keeps it so (How to listen on the LAN). Every request is a scrape or a password check, and either costs the router CPU. A client that reaches the port without the right credentials still makes the handler check the ones it sends. uhttpd runs 3 requests at once and keeps at most 10 connections. So such a client delays the scrapes, and no more: requests past those wait their turn, and the connection limit bounds how many can wait. See HTTP endpoint.

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text:
• The jail is not a sandbox against a hostile collector. It narrows what the installed collectors can reach, and its user narrows what they can do; it does not vet them. A collector package is code you choose to run: see Buggy, not hostile.
  • The same jail everywhere it can be had. check, the ubus object's status and prometheus-exporter scrape run the collectors in the service's own jail, with ujail: as its user, with the capabilities the service has, and under the ACL it wrote. So what they find is what Prometheus gets. While the service is stopped, they run without those capabilities and that ACL. Where ujail cannot run (not root, or a kernel or container that refuses it a namespace), they run outside the jail, as root, and say so; the guards are the same. prometheus-exporter collector check runs a module not installed yet, outside the jail. chronyd's server statistics are read only when these run outside the jail: reaching them means writing to chronyd's command directory, which the jail does not give.
  • rpcd runs the ubus object unjailed. It reads the committed configuration and writes nothing but the hash, through set_password. It and hash_password alone handle a secret, and they log neither the secret nor the hash. The LuCI app's ACL grants the reading methods, and grants set_password only to a login that may write.
  • A password changed in LuCI applies at once, without LuCI's rollback. set_password commits the hash and reloads the service when Change password is pressed, apart from Save & Apply, which cannot undo it. A scraper that is not given the new password fails until it is. LuCI's own router password is changed the same way.

docs.title: About Versioned Documentation
docs.text: The documentation describes a package that people install and then keep running for months. A router on last year's release should be able to read the docs of last year's release, and a reader who just arrived should land on the newest. This page explains how the publishing setup serves both, and why it is stricter than it first looks. The machinery itself is described in Documentation publishing.

docs.title: One version per minor, and only one maintained
docs.text:
The site has a folder per minor release, /0.1/, /0.2/, and /latest/ for the newest. Patch releases do not get their own folder; they overwrite their minor. A patch release changes behaviour in small ways at most. A reader choosing between 0.2.0, 0.2.1 and 0.2.2 in a version selector would gain nothing but a longer list. The title of each version still shows the exact release it was built from.

The exporter is a small project, and it maintains exactly one version: the newest. That shapes the docs too. Old versions stay online, because someone is running them, but they are frozen at their last publish. Only the newest version's docs get fixes. Backporting doc fixes to every old minor would be a promise the project cannot keep. A half-kept promise is worse than a clear rule: a reader of /0.1/ knows it is a record of 0.1, not a living page.

The other half of the rule is that the docs of unreleased work are never published. main often describes behaviour no release has yet. Publishing it, even under a dev label, would put the most visible, most search-indexed pages ahead of the code people can actually install. So main and pull requests only build the site, strictly, to catch broken links early; they never publish it. The docs go online with the release they describe.

docs.title: Why the docs branches exist
docs.text:
A release tag is immutable, and so are the docs inside it. But the docs of a release will have mistakes: a typo, a wrong default, a missing step. Waiting for the next release to fix them leaves readers with the error for weeks, and cutting a release just for a doc fix spends a version number on something that is not a change to the package.

A docs/X.Y branch is the way out. It starts at the release tag, vX.Y.0, and carries doc fixes on top of it. Pushing it republishes /X.Y/. The branch is not a release branch and never becomes one: it exists only to let the published docs of a released version get better without a new release.

docs.title: Why the branch must stay docs-only
docs.text:
The danger of a branch that sits next to a release is that it slowly becomes one. A small code fix gets cherry-picked "just this once", the docs describe it, and now the published docs of 0.2 describe code that is not in any 0.2 package. Anyone reading them and running the real 0.2 sees something else. Worse, the branch now holds a version of the code that no tag names, and nobody can say which fixes it has.

The guard makes that impossible rather than discouraged. Before a docs branch publishes, it compares the branch with its release tag and refuses if anything outside the docs changed. The code in a docs branch is therefore always exactly the code of a release, and the only way to ship a code fix is a release, with a tag, a version number and a changelog entry. The refusal message says as much: "code fixes need a release".

The guard also insists that the newest release tag of the minor is an ancestor of the branch. After a patch release, the branch has to move onto the new tag before it can publish again. Otherwise a docs fix pushed to an old branch would overwrite the patch release's docs with the docs of the previous patch, silently undoing whatever the patch changed.

Tags are not guarded. A tag is the release; its docs are by definition the docs of that release.

docs.title: Why fixes go to main first, and why never rebase
docs.text:
A doc fix that only lands on the docs branch is lost at the next minor, which is cut from main. So a fix lands on main first, and is cherry-picked onto the docs branch. That keeps main the one place every fix lives, and makes the docs branch a strict subset: its release, plus a few commits that are already on main.

Merging or rebasing main into the docs branch looks like a shortcut, but it brings along everything else on main, including the docs of unreleased features. The guard catches the code that comes with them, but not the docs, which it allows by design. Cherry-picking is deliberate: each commit that reaches a published version was chosen for it.

Merging a patch release's tag into the docs branch is a different thing. The tag is a release, so everything it brings has shipped. That is why moving the branch to a patch tag is a fast-forward or a merge, while main never goes in.

When the next minor ships, its branch takes over and the old one is frozen. Nothing stops a push to the old branch, but the one-maintained-version rule means there is no reason to.

docs.title: Why latest only moves forward
docs.text:
latest is what most readers see. It must always be the newest release, whatever order publishes happen in. Publishes do happen out of order: a fix to an older version, or a manual republish of one, can run after the newer minor has shipped. If every publish took latest, republishing 0.1 would silently point the whole site back at an old release.

So a publish takes latest only if its version is the newest one on gh-pages. The comparison is by version, not by text, because 0.10 is newer than 0.9 and a text sort says otherwise. Publishes also run one at a time, since two mike deploys racing on the same branch could each overwrite the other's work.

docs.title: Pinned links and latest links
docs.text:
A link to the docs is either about the project now or about a particular release. The README and a forum answer are about now: they should follow the project, so they link to /latest/. A changelog entry, a release note, or a URL inside the package is about one release, and has to keep pointing at the docs of that release after newer ones come out.

The package matters most. A router running 0.1 that shows a help URL should lead to the 0.1 docs, where the options and messages match what is installed, not to the newest docs, which may describe options it does not have. Pinning the shipped links to the package's minor gives every installed version a link to its own docs.

Pinned links rot silently: bump the version and forget one link, and the next release ships pointing at the previous minor. A check in make lint catches that. The changelog gets the same check per section, and [Unreleased] allows no pinned link at all, because the version it will be released as is not known yet.

Links between pages of the docs are always relative. A relative link resolves inside whatever version the reader is in, so each published version is self-contained without any rewriting.

docs.title: The redirect for old links
docs.text: A link without a version, /<site>/how-to/..., is an easy one to write by hand, and any link from before the site was versioned looks like that. Nothing lives at those paths any more. Rather than breaking every such link, the site's 404 page moves a missing unversioned path under /latest/, keeping its query and anchor. A path that is already inside a version folder is left as a real "not found": redirecting it could loop, and a page that does not exist in 0.1 should not quietly become a page of another version.

docs.title: Why mkdocs.yml stays free of mike
docs.text: The versioned settings live in their own file, mkdocs.mike.yml, which inherits mkdocs.yml. With the mike plugin and version provider in the main config, a plain mkdocs serve would show a version selector with nothing behind it, and every writer's preview would depend on mike. Keeping them apart means writing and previewing the docs needs nothing but MkDocs Material, and the versioned build is exercised on its own in CI and by make -C docs build-mike.

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text:
latest is a copy. mike can make an alias a symlink, a redirect page, or a copy. GitHub Pages cannot be relied on to serve symlinks, and redirect pages would make every /latest/ URL a hop through a stub. A copy gives real pages at stable URLs. The price is that every page of the newest version exists twice; the canonical URL of each page points to its /latest/ copy, so search engines can treat the two as one. Identical files are stored once in git, so the copy costs little on gh-pages.

The 404 redirect assumes a project site. It treats the first path segment as the site, which matches https://<user>.github.io/<site>/. On a custom domain or a user site, where the docs live at the root, the redirect would need changing.

CI and local builds use different installs. Local builds run the pinned mkdocs-material image, plus mike in a derived image. The publish job installs the same pinned mkdocs-material and mike with pip on the runner, which spares CI building the image. But their own dependencies are not pinned, so a dependency release can make CI's build differ from a local one. Both builds are strict, so the likely failure is a loud one, not a quiet difference in the published site.

The freeze is a rule, not a lock. Nothing technical stops a push to an old docs branch; the guard only keeps it docs-only. The project relies on the one-maintained-version rule for the rest.

docs.title: About Versions
docs.text: Releases are semantic versions, X.Y.Z, tagged vX.Y.Z. This page is about what each part promises to someone who builds on the exporter, and how the packages and the documentation follow the version.

docs.title: What a version promises
docs.text:
People build on the exporter in several ways: queries and dashboards on its metric names, scripts on its uci options and ubus methods, collectors on its collector interface, images on its package names. A version says which of those can break.

  • Major: a metric, label or metric type renamed or removed; a uci option renamed, removed or meaning something else; a ubus method's arguments or replies changed incompatibly; collect(deps, out, options), meta or the collector API changed incompatibly (a name it exports removed, or meaning something else); a package or group renamed or split.
  • Minor: new collectors, metrics, labels on new families, options, ubus methods, names the collector API exports, and new cases of nothing to observe.
  • Patch: fixes, speed, and documentation.

A new case of nothing to observe is a minor change, though it changes what a scrape says of a collector: a collector that failed on some device now succeeds there, with node_scrape_collector_observing 0. Nothing that worked stops working, and an alert on failures fires less, for the right reason.

A value that was wrong is fixed in a patch, and the CHANGELOG says so: a counter that counted the wrong thing, or a gauge in the wrong unit. Queries on it change, but they were reading a bug.

docs.title: What 1.0 keeps
docs.text:
0.3.0 is the release candidate for 1.0. Everything below is as 1.0 will have it. From 0.3.0 on, a release adds to it and fixes it, and only a major version breaks it.

What Kept Listed in Metrics Each family's name, type, labels, unit and meaning, the exporter's own (node_scrape_collector_*, ucode_prometheus_exporter_*) included. Metrics, Collectors Collectors and packages Each collector's name and module, as collect[] and the uci sections name them. The packages' and groups' names, and that a group pulls in the collectors it has. Collectors, Files and packages Configuration The sections and options of /etc/config/prometheus-exporter and /etc/config/prometheus-exporter-auth: their names, the values they take, and what they mean. UCI configuration HTTP endpoint /metrics, its query parameters, the scrape-timeout header, gzip, and basic auth over HTTPS. HTTP endpoint ubus objects The methods of prometheus-exporter and prometheus-exporter.filesystem: their arguments, and the fields of their replies. ubus object The command prometheus-exporter's commands, options and exit statuses, and what scrape prints, which is a scrape. The prometheus-exporter command Error codes Each code and its meaning. They are values of the reason label of ucode_prometheus_exporter_collector_failures_total, and of ubus replies. Error codes The collector API What a collector of another package builds on: below. Collector interface, The devkit Alerting rules Each alert's name and its severity, which Alertmanager routes on. Bundled dashboards and alerts

Adding to any of these is a minor version: a field of a ubus reply, an option, a collector, an alert. A query, script or route that worked keeps working.

No version promises the rest. Any release may change:

  • the log messages' wording and priority (Log messages). Alert on the metrics, not on the log;
  • what check, collector list and collector check print for a person to read;
  • the LuCI app's pages and texts;
  • the core's modules, behind the collector API;
  • the files the service writes while it runs, under /var/run/prometheus-exporter;
  • an alert's expression and threshold, and the dashboards' panels;
  • how fast the exporter is, and the memory and flash it takes.

docs.title: The collector API
docs.text:
A collector imports one module, prometheus.exporter, and the loader refuses one that imports any other (see Collector contract). That makes the API, beside meta, collect and the capabilities in deps, the whole of what a collector builds on in the exporter's code. What it exports is what a major version protects. The modules behind it, prometheus.exporter.result, .proc and the rest, are the core's. Any release may split, rename or change them as the core needs, because no collector can have imported them.

Without that rule, every module a collector happened to import would be a promise, and the core could not move a function without a major version, or would break a collector of someone else's package without knowing. The API lists, name by name, what is promised; the rest is free.

What a collector of another package builds on is, all of it:

  • The collector API, the module prometheus.exporter: Result, errors, services, proc (rows among them), exposition, u16 and u32, each name it exports.
  • Where a collector is: /usr/share/ucode/prometheus/collectors/<module>.uc, which its package installs, the module prometheus.collectors.<module>, which its tests import.
  • The recorder, out: gauge, counter, untyped, batch, labels and parse, and what each records.
  • meta: its fields and what each means, those the jail derives grants from (paths, configs, commands, ubus, capabilities, groups, proc_files) included; and deps, each capability's functions.
  • The rules a module is loaded by: strict mode, the API alone, and a top level that only declares, with the functions it may call there.
  • The devkit, what a collector's tests build on: its modules, prometheus.exporter.devkit.collector, .fixtures, .commands and .rc, and their exports; with_collector's config and run; and its proxies, under /usr/share/ucode/prometheus/exporter/devkit/proxies/, their keys and channels.

0.3.0 froze them for 1.0, with the rest of what 1.0 keeps: a later 0.x adds to them, and only a major version breaks one. So a collector package depends on the exporter's major from 1.0 (>=1.0.0), and on 0.3.0 or later before it, rather than on the exact release the exporter's own packages pin.

docs.title: Before 1.0.0
docs.text:
In 0.1 and 0.2, a minor version could break any of these, and said so. The metric names and the configuration were still settling, and holding them fixed then would have frozen mistakes.

0.3.0 settled them. From 0.3.0 on, a 0.x release breaks nothing of what 1.0 keeps, as if it were already 1.x. So a router on 0.3 upgrades to 1.0 as to a minor version, and the dashboards, alerts, scripts and collectors written for 0.3 keep working.

1.0.0 is meant to be the first release to OpenWrt's packages feed. It adds nothing that breaks 0.3.

docs.title: The package version
docs.text:
PKG_VERSION in the package Makefile is the release, 0.1.0. PKG_RELEASE, the -rN of 0.1.0-r1, counts changes to the packaging alone, a dependency or an install step, and starts again at 1 with each version. ucode_prometheus_exporter_build_info{version="0.1.0-r1"} reports both.

Every collector package, group and the LuCI app depends on the base package of the very same <version>-r<release>. A collector runs on the exporter's internals, and the LuCI app calls its ubus methods as that release has them. Allowing a mix would mean testing every combination, and supporting the ones nobody tested. So an upgrade moves every package at once.

docs.title: The documentation's versions
docs.text: The documentation is published per minor release, /0.1/, /0.2/, with /latest/ for the newest, as About versioned documentation explains. A patch release replaces its minor's docs, since a patch changes no option, metric or method. A router on 0.1 reads the 0.1 docs, where the options and metrics are the ones it has.

docs.title: What Happens When a Collector Breaks
docs.text: The exporter runs each scrape's collectors in a process of their own. It holds each collector to a budget and the scrape to the scraper's timeout, and it sets aside a collector that keeps failing (see About deadlines and circuit breakers). This page measures what that buys: the same faults, given to this exporter and to the feed's Lua exporter, as a real Prometheus server scrapes them.

docs.title: The scenarios
docs.text:
Each is a fault a router meets, not one made up for the exporter:

  • A hung ubus daemon. netifd's network.wireless, hostapd's hostapd.wlan0 and dnsmasq's object are registered, but the daemon behind them sleeps at the first call, and never answers it or any after it: a daemon stuck in a driver's call or a lock. ubusd still lists the objects and hands them each call. Both exporters' wifi, hostapd and dnsmasq collectors call them.
  • A stuck program. nft never exits, as when a large ruleset holds the netlink lock. Both exporters' nft counters collectors run it. Any program a collector runs would do; this is one both exporters run.
  • A label that is not UTF-8. A static DHCP lease's name is caf\xe9, "café" in Latin-1, which uci takes as it is. Both exporters' uci_dhcp_host collectors put it in a label.
  • A huge conntrack table on a slow router. 20,000 connections, as 64 LAN hosts open them to the internet through the router's NAT. The table is on a MIPS 24Kc in QEMU (OpenWrt's malta target), as fast as make bench-qemu's 500-MIPS guest. Both exporters' nat_traffic collectors read the whole table at each scrape.

And one scenario where nothing is wrong, to compare with.

Each exporter has every collector package of its own that installs on the system: for this exporter, the base package and the -full group; for the Lua exporter, each of its collector packages that installs no service. Prometheus scrapes them every 15 s with its default scrape_timeout, 10 s, eight times a scenario.

docs.title: The results
docs.text:
make failure-demo, on OpenWrt 25.12.5: this exporter as 0.3.0 has it, before the release, and the feed's prometheus-node-exporter-lua 2026.06.05-r1, scraped by Prometheus 3.15.0. The conntrack scenario ran in QEMU; the others ran in containers on an x86-64 laptop.

Scenario Exporter Scrapes up Scrape duration Samples Prometheus's last error nothing wrong this one 8 of 8 0.06 to 0.07 s 1191 to 1194 — nothing wrong Lua 8 of 8 0.01 to 0.03 s 897 — hung ubus daemon this one 8 of 8 9.50 s, once 5.07 s 445 (the first two), then 1012 to 1167 — hung ubus daemon Lua 0 of 7 10.0 s 0 context deadline exceeded stuck program this one 8 of 8 5.07 s (3 scrapes), else 0.05 to 0.06 s 1192 to 1195 — stuck program Lua 0 of 8 10.0 s 0 context deadline exceeded label not UTF-8 this one 8 of 8 0.05 to 0.06 s 1192 to 1195 — label not UTF-8 Lua 0 of 8 0.02 to 0.03 s 888 invalid UTF-8 label value: "\"caf\xe9\"" 20,000 connections, QEMU this one 8 of 8 7.11 s, then 1.43 to 2.13 s, and 6.58 and 6.73 s (nat_traffic tried again) 820 to 823 — 20,000 connections, QEMU Lua 0 of 7 10.0 s 0 context deadline exceeded

What each exporter says of itself: the collectors that failed in the last scrape Prometheus got, and the exporter's log. And, at the end, one scrape from the router, with no timeout but uhttpd's own:

Scenario Exporter Failed, last scrape The log A scrape without a timeout nothing wrong this one none nothing 0.06 s, 1195 samples, 36 collectors nothing wrong Lua dawn dawn's error, every scrape (no dawn daemon) 0.01 s, 898 samples, 27 collectors hung ubus daemon this one dnsmasq, exporter, hostapd_stations, hostapd_ubus_stations, wifi COLLECTOR_CANCELLED and a quarantine for each of the four; scrape deadline: 28 collectors not served, then 2 to 6 9.50 s, 1014 samples, 36 collectors hung ubus daemon Lua — hostapd_stations' error, 30 s into a scrape a reply cut off after 30.0 s: 237 samples, 7 of its 27 collectors stuck program this one nft-counters COMMAND_TIMEOUT (nft: still running after 5 s, killed), quarantined for 1, 2, then 4 scrapes 0.07 s, 1196 samples, 36 collectors stuck program Lua — nothing a reply cut off after 30.0 s: 651 samples, 16 of 27 collectors label not UTF-8 this one uci_dhcp_host EXPOSITION_INVALID (in node_openwrt_dhcp_host_info, label 'name': its value is not valid UTF-8), quarantined for 1, 2, then 4 scrapes 0.07 s, 1196 samples, 36 collectors label not UTF-8 Lua — nothing 0.02 s, 899 samples, 27 collectors: Prometheus refuses it whole 20,000 connections this one nat_traffic COLLECTOR_CANCELLED (still running after 5.00 s, over its budget of 5 s: stopped), quarantined for 1, 2, then 4 scrapes 2.30 s, 823 samples, 36 collectors 20,000 connections Lua — nothing 12.7 s, 20806 samples, 27 collectors: complete, and too late

The QEMU guests ran ucode's loop turn at 7.5 µs with the Lua exporter and 11.3 µs with this one, about 660 and 440 MIPS of a 24Kc. So the Lua exporter had the faster guest.

docs.title: What it comes to
docs.text:
A collector that hangs, in each exporter:

flowchart LR
    H[a collector hangs] --> L1[Lua: the request waits on it]
    L1 --> L2[Prometheus gives up at 10 s]
    L2 --> L3[up 0, every series of the router gone]
    H --> T1[this one: stopped at its budget, 5 s]
    T1 --> T2[the rest served within the deadline]
    T1 --> T3[breaker trips: quarantined for 1, 2, 4 ... 32 scrapes]

The Lua exporter copes with none of the four, and this one copes with each, at a cost. The Lua exporter's collectors run one after the other in the request's process, with no time limit of their own. Whatever one waits on, the whole scrape waits on, and Prometheus gives up at 10 s with nothing. The Lua exporter's libubus calls do time out after 30 s, as does uhttpd's wait for output (its -T, 30 s), but both are three times Prometheus's timeout. Without a scraper's timeout, the reply ends after 30 s, cut off where the collector stalled, and the collectors after it are missing. A label that is not UTF-8 is written as it is, and Prometheus refuses the whole scrape for it, every time.

This exporter answers every scrape in time, and serves what it can. Once the broken collector's breaker has tripped, each scenario costs it that collector alone:

  • The stuck program is killed at its timeout, 5 s. The collector fails with COMMAND_TIMEOUT and is quarantined for 1, 2, 4 scrapes and up to 32. The scrapes that try it again take 5 s; the others take 0.06 s.
  • The label is refused where it is written (EXPOSITION_INVALID). The collector's samples are left out, and the rest of the reply is valid.
  • On the slow router, nat_traffic is stopped at its budget, 5 s, and quarantined. The first scrape takes 7.1 s, those that try it again 6.6 to 6.7 s, and the others 1.4 to 2.1 s, with every other collector served. The Lua exporter writes the whole table, a series per pair of addresses, 20,806 samples, in 12.7 s: Prometheus has given up by then, at 10.
  • A hung ubus daemon costs more, and for longer. Four collectors call it, and each runs until its budget, 5 s, and is stopped (COLLECTOR_CANCELLED). The first two scrapes after the start come before the ledger knows any collector's time, so they run those four among the others. One is stopped at its budget, the next at the deadline, and the 28 collectors not yet run are left out (445 samples of 1191). From the third scrape on, the collectors that answer run first, and the scrape loses only the hung ones. But with four of them, each quarantined in turn, one is tried in nearly every scrape. So the scrapes take 9.5 s of Prometheus's 10, as their deadline allows, until the cool-downs grow past the four. At 32 scrapes of cool-down each, that is a trial every 8 scrapes or so.

docs.title: What the user sees
docs.text:
Scenario This exporter The Lua exporter A hung ubus daemon OpenWrtExporterCollectorQuarantined and ...CollectorFailing for each collector that calls it, OpenWrtExporterScrapeSlow while scrapes take 9.5 s, OpenWrtExporterDeadlineSkips; COLLECTOR_CANCELLED in the log. The router's other metrics keep coming. up 0: OpenWrtExporterDown, with nothing to say which collector, and every series of the router gone. A stuck program OpenWrtExporterProgramTimeouts and ...CollectorQuarantined; COMMAND_TIMEOUT in the log, naming the program. up 0, with nothing to say which collector. A label that is not UTF-8 OpenWrtExporterCollectorFailing; EXPOSITION_INVALID in the log, naming the family and the label. up 0, with Prometheus's error naming the value, on the Targets page. A huge conntrack table OpenWrtExporterCollectorQuarantined and ...CollectorFailing for nat_traffic; COLLECTOR_CANCELLED in the log. The answer is a job of its own for nat_traffic, with a longer timeout and a budget to match, or leaving it out: Performance on small routers. up 0.

The alerts are those of How to monitor a router with the bundled dashboards and alerts. The codes are in Error codes, and the log lines in Log messages. With the Lua exporter, the failure Prometheus sees is the target down. To find which collector failed, scrape it by hand with a longer timeout, one collect[] at a time.

docs.title: What the numbers do not say
docs.text:
• The containers are not routers. Both exporters run as their init scripts start them, uhttpd with the same options, but without procd: with no jail, and as root, so that the containers need no privileges. ubusd, logd and rpcd run; stand-ins answer for netifd, procd and dnsmasq. The QEMU guests boot OpenWrt and run each exporter's service under procd.
  • The Lua exporter's healthy scrape is faster: 0.02 s where this one takes 0.06 s, on a laptop. This exporter forks a process for its collectors and has 9 more of them; see Performance on small routers.
  • QEMU is not a router either. Without -icount, the guest's clock is the host's, so that Prometheus, outside, measures what the guest takes. The guest's speed is then the host's share of a CPU. That share is set so that a turn of a ucode loop takes about what it takes make bench-qemu's 500-MIPS 24Kc, 9.9 µs, and it is printed with each run. It varies between runs with the host's load.

docs.title: How to reproduce it
docs.text:
make failure-demo                           # every scenario, some 25 minutes
make failure-demo FD_SCENARIOS="hung-ubus"  # one; healthy, hung-ubus, stuck-nft, bad-utf8, conntrack

It builds the packages, and an image with the Lua exporter's packages beside this one's. It runs each scenario's two exporters in containers of their own, unprivileged, on a network of their own, with a Prometheus server (the official image) that scrapes them. The conntrack scenario boots each exporter in QEMU in turn. It needs the network, for the images and for the release's packages for the QEMU guests. It prints the tables above, and keeps them in bin/failure-demo/, with each exporter's log and the JSON it read from Prometheus's API. Every container goes when it ends. FD_SCRAPES sets the scrapes of each scenario, FD_CONNTRACK the table's connections, and FD_QEMU_CPUS the share of a CPU the guest gets: see Make targets. The scripts are devenv/scripts/failure-demo.sh and devenv/scripts/failure-demo/.

docs.title: How to Monitor AdGuard Home
docs.text:
The agh collector reads two endpoints of AdGuard Home's HTTP API on the router:

  • /control/status: whether AdGuard Home runs and protects
  • /control/stats: the totals of its statistics window

It reads them without a login, at an address of the router.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• AdGuard Home runs on the router (adguardhome), enabled, and its setup is done.
  • Its web interface has no users: users: [] in /etc/adguardhome/adguardhome.yaml. The collector sends no credentials. See If it fails.
  • ucode-prometheus-exporter-agh is installed. It brings ucode-mod-socket, but not AdGuard Home.

docs.title: 1. Point the collector at AdGuard Home's web interface
docs.text:
By default, the collector connects to 127.0.0.1, port 8080. Find where AdGuard Home listens: http.address in its config.

grep -A12 '^http:' /etc/adguardhome/adguardhome.yaml | grep address

  address: 0.0.0.0:8080
  • 0.0.0.0 or 127.0.0.1, port 8080: nothing to do.
  • Another port, such as the setup's 3000: set port.
  • One address of the router, such as 192.168.1.1:8080, which OpenWrt's guide to AdGuard Home has you choose: set address to it. AdGuard Home then does not answer on 127.0.0.1.
uci set prometheus-exporter.agh=collector
uci set prometheus-exporter.agh.address=192.168.1.1
uci set prometheus-exporter.agh.port=8080
uci commit prometheus-exporter
service prometheus-exporter reload

address must be an address of the router itself, IPv4 or IPv6. The collector refuses any other address, without connecting (see About the security model).

docs.title: 2. Check it
docs.text:
wget -qO- 'http://127.0.0.1:9100/metrics?collect[]=agh' | grep '^adguard_'

adguard_up 1
adguard_build_info{version="0.107.79"} 1
adguard_running 1
adguard_protection_enabled 1
adguard_start_time_seconds 1792437171.9284565
adguard_stats_window_seconds 86400
adguard_stats_dns_queries 14496
adguard_stats_blocked_filtering 1482
...

Metrics lists the families and what each means.

docs.title: Query the statistics window
docs.text:
/control/stats gives totals over AdGuard Home's statistics window, not counters since it started. The window is the last 24 hours by default (its statistics.interval). As the window moves, the oldest hour drops out, and a total can fall.

So the collector writes them as gauges, adguard_stats_*, not as _total counters, along with the window's length, adguard_stats_window_seconds. Do not use rate() or increase() on them: these take a fall for a counter reset, and would count the whole total again. Query them as gauges:

For Query Queries in the last 24 hours adguard_stats_dns_queries Queries a second, averaged over the window adguard_stats_dns_queries / adguard_stats_window_seconds Share blocked by the filters adguard_stats_blocked_filtering / adguard_stats_dns_queries Blocked by safe browsing and parental control adguard_stats_replaced_safebrowsing + adguard_stats_replaced_parental Mean answer time adguard_stats_avg_processing_time_seconds AdGuard Home down, or not answering adguard_up == 0, or node_scrape_collector_success{collector="agh"} == 0 Filtering paused adguard_protection_enabled == 0

You cannot get a rate over a few minutes. The window's totals move by the hour, as AdGuard Home rolls its hourly units. For counters of every query, read AdGuard Home's query log, or use a resolver that counts, as Unbound does.

The collector writes nothing about the domains, clients and upstreams that AdGuard Home ranks (top_queried_domains, top_clients, top_blocked_domains). They would need one series each, without bound, and would expose what the people on the network browse.

docs.title: From dashboards of other names
docs.text:
Some scripts for the textfile collector wrote node_adguard_* names. A dashboard built on those names needs these changes:

Was Is Change node_adguard_up adguard_up The name. node_adguard_dns_queries_total adguard_stats_dns_queries The name; and rate() or increase() of it, a window's total, becomes the gauge itself, or its ratio to adguard_stats_window_seconds. node_adguard_blocked_filtering_total adguard_stats_blocked_filtering As the queries. node_adguard_avg_processing_seconds adguard_stats_avg_processing_time_seconds The name.

docs.title: If it fails
docs.text: check or the log says Cause agh has nothing to observe: adguardhome is not installed, or is disabled Nothing answered, and AdGuard Home is not installed, or its init script is disabled. Nothing is wrong. SOCKET_FAILED (127.0.0.1:8080: connect(): Connection refused) AdGuard Home is enabled and does not listen there: it is stopped, or listens on another address or port. Step 1. SOCKET_FAILED (192.0.2.1:8080: 192.0.2.1 is not an address of this device, ...) address is not one of the router's. SOURCE_UNREADABLE (...: AdGuard Home asks for a login (401 Unauthorized), ...) AdGuard Home has users. The collector reads only one without: a password it could send would sit where the service's user, and every collector, reads it, and the exporter keeps no secret there. SOURCE_INVALID (...: not a JSON object), (...: 404 Not Found) Something else answers at that address and port, as LuCI's uhttpd on port 80.

docs.title: How to Choose Collectors
docs.text:
Three things decide what a scrape holds:

  • which collector packages are installed
  • which collectors are enabled
  • what each scrape asks for

docs.title: Install collectors
docs.text:
Install a collector's package, or a group of them:

Browser (LuCI)Terminal (SSH)
  1. Open System → Software and press Update lists….
  2. Type the package's name in Filter, such as ucode-prometheus-exporter-wireguard or the group ucode-prometheus-exporter-network.
  3. On the Available tab, press Install… on its row, then Install in the dialog.
apk add ucode-prometheus-exporter-wireguard
apk add ucode-prometheus-exporter-network

The service reloads with the new collector. Collectors lists each collector, its package, its groups and what it depends on.

Some collectors are in no group, so only their own package installs them:

  • the collectors for particular hardware or services
  • interrupts, which node_exporter turns off by default because it writes many series, one per interrupt and CPU
  • pressure, which needs a kernel with CONFIG_PSI, which OpenWrt's kernels leave off

Installing the package turns the collector on, as above: ucode-prometheus-exporter-interrupts, for example.

pressure has nothing to observe without /proc/pressure. Install it only on a kernel built with CONFIG_PSI, and not booted with psi=0. Check for the directory first, over SSH:

ls /proc/pressure
apk add ucode-prometheus-exporter-pressure

docs.title: Disable a collector
docs.text:
You can stop serving any installed collector, including a base collector.

Browser (LuCI)Terminal (SSH)
  1. Open Services → Prometheus exporter, tab Collectors. It lists the collectors by title: softnet is Network softirq statistics.
  2. Untick the collector in the Enabled column.
  3. Press Save & Apply.

See How to use the LuCI app.

Set enabled to 0 in the collector's section. The section is named after the collector's module: the collector's name with _ for -, such as ltq_dsl for ltq-dsl.

uci set prometheus-exporter.softnet=collector
uci set prometheus-exporter.softnet.enabled=0
uci commit prometheus-exporter
service prometheus-exporter reload

The exporter does not run a disabled collector, and the jail mounts nothing for it. A scrape that names it in collect[] gets a 400. To serve it again:

Browser (LuCI)Terminal (SSH)

Tick the collector again in the Enabled column, and press Save & Apply.

Set enabled back to 1, or delete the collector's section if nothing else is set there:

uci delete prometheus-exporter.softnet
uci commit prometheus-exporter
service prometheus-exporter reload

docs.title: Remove a collector
docs.text: Remove its package: see How to remove the exporter.

docs.title: Choose per scrape
docs.text:
To make one scrape job take only some collectors, give Prometheus the query parameters:

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: openwrt-wifi
    params:
      collect[]: [ wifi, hostapd_stations ]
    static_configs:
      - targets: [ 'router.lan:9100' ]

exclude[] leaves collectors out instead. The scrape fails with a 400 if it names a collector that is not installed, or names a disabled one in collect[]. See HTTP endpoint.

docs.title: Check
docs.text:
Browser (LuCI)Terminal (SSH)

The Collectors tab of Services → Prometheus exporter says how many collectors are enabled, as 15 of 16 collectors enabled. Status → Prometheus exporter lists each collector, with Not run: switched off for a disabled one.

service prometheus-exporter status
service prometheus-exporter check

status counts the collectors served. check lists each collector, enabled or not.

docs.title: How to Monitor chrony
docs.text:
Two collectors watch the clock when chronyd keeps it:

  • timesync, in the base package, says whether the clock is synchronized, whichever daemon keeps it: busybox ntpd or chronyd. It writes node_timesync_synchronized{daemon="chronyd"}, and the daemon's stratum, offset and last update.
  • chrony, in its own package, writes chronyd's details with chrony_exporter's names: its tracking, each source, and its server statistics where it serves time.

Use timesync to alert when the clock is not synchronized. Add chrony to see why.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• chrony is installed and running: the chrony (or chrony-nts) package, its service enabled, and its servers in /etc/config/chrony.
  • The base package is installed.

docs.title: 1. Install the chrony collector
docs.text:
apk add ucode-prometheus-exporter-chrony

The service reloads with it.

docs.title: 2. Check it
docs.text:
service prometheus-exporter check | grep -e chrony -e timesync
wget -qO- 'http://127.0.0.1:9100/metrics?collect[]=chrony&collect[]=timesync' | grep -e '^chrony_tracking_stratum' -e '^node_timesync_synchronized'

chrony_tracking_stratum 3
node_timesync_synchronized{daemon="chronyd"} 1

If busybox ntpd runs too, timesync writes a series for each daemon: daemon="ntpd" and daemon="chronyd". Only one should keep the clock. Turn the system's NTP client off, in LuCI's System → System → Time Synchronization or with uci set system.ntp.enabled=0.

docs.title: Server statistics
docs.text:
A scrape of /metrics never holds chronyd's server statistics, chrony_serverstats_*. Here is why:

  • chronyd answers them only on its Unix command socket.
  • chronyc reaches that socket only by creating a socket of its own beside it, in /var/run/chrony.
  • Write access there would let the exporter command chronyd, which sets the clock. So the exporter's jail does not give it.

Under procd, the collector asks over chronyd's UDP command port instead, as chronyc falls back to. That port answers tracking and sources, but not the server statistics.

prometheus-exporter scrape chrony also runs in the service's jail, so it does not show them either. To see them on the device, ask chronyd:

chronyc serverstats

docs.title: If it fails
docs.text:
check or the log says Cause chrony has nothing to observe: chronyd is disabled chronyd's init script is disabled. Nothing is wrong. chrony: COMMAND_FAILED (chronyc: exit status 1) chronyd is enabled and does not answer: it is stopped, or does not answer on its command port. timesync has nothing to observe: neither ntpd nor chronyd runs No NTP daemon runs. timesync: SOURCE_UNREADABLE (chronyd is enabled and not running) chronyd is enabled at boot, and stopped.

See Collectors and Metrics.

docs.title: How to Set a Collector's Options
docs.text: Some collectors take options of their own, such as wifi's stations, dhcp_leases' leases, vmstat's fields, diskstats' device_exclude, textfile's directory and unbound's socket. Collectors lists each collector's options with their defaults. service prometheus-exporter check prints each option with its help and value.

docs.title: Set an option
docs.text:
Browser (LuCI)Terminal (SSH)
  1. Open Services → Prometheus exporter, tab Collectors.
  2. Press Edit on the collector's row, such as Wi-Fi. The dialog shows each option by its title, with its help: wifi's stations is Station metrics.

  3. Change the field, and press Save. The values are staged, not applied.

  4. Press Save & Apply on the page.

A collector's options go in its section of /etc/config/prometheus-exporter. The section is named after the collector's module: the collector's name with _ for -.

uci set prometheus-exporter.wifi=collector
uci set prometheus-exporter.wifi.stations=0
uci commit prometheus-exporter
service prometheus-exporter reload

The section's type must be collector. If there is no section, or the option is not in it, the collector uses its default.

docs.title: Check the value
docs.text:
Browser (LuCI)Terminal (SSH)

The Edit dialog checks each value as the exporter would. If the collector does not take a value, Save stages nothing, says Nothing was staged: the exporter would refuse these values., and marks the field with why.

service prometheus-exporter check

check prints a FAIL line for a value the collector does not take, such as collector wifi, section 'wifi': CONFIG_INVALID (stations: expected a boolean, got "maybe"), and exits 1. The collector fails in every scrape until you fix the value.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In LuCI, each example is one field of the collector's Edit dialog, named with the example. Over SSH, run the commands, then uci commit prometheus-exporter and service prometheus-exporter reload.

Leave out wifi's per-station metrics, which grow with the clients. In LuCI, untick Station metrics in Wi-Fi's dialog:

uci set prometheus-exporter.wifi=collector
uci set prometheus-exporter.wifi.stations=0

Have dhcp_leases write a series per lease, with its address, MAC and hostname. In LuCI, tick Lease series in DHCP leases's dialog:

uci set prometheus-exporter.dhcp_leases=collector
uci set prometheus-exporter.dhcp_leases.leases=1

Export more of /proc/vmstat, by a regular expression of its field names. In LuCI, set Exported fields in Virtual memory statistics's dialog:

uci set prometheus-exporter.vmstat=collector
uci set prometheus-exporter.vmstat.fields='^(oom_kill|pgpg|pswp|pg.*fault|nr_free_pages).*'

Watch the partitions of an eMMC or SD card too, which diskstats leaves out by default. This still leaves out flash, loop devices and zram. In LuCI, set Excluded devices in Disk I/O's dialog:

uci set prometheus-exporter.diskstats=collector
uci set prometheus-exporter.diskstats.device_exclude='^(z?ram|loop|mtdblock|ubiblock[0-9]+_)[0-9]+$'

device_exclude is a POSIX extended regular expression, as ucode compiles it. ^$ leaves out no device.

docs.title: In LuCI
docs.text:
The Browser (LuCI) tabs above use the collector's Edit dialog, on the Collectors tab of Services → Prometheus exporter. Save stages the values, and Save & Apply applies them. See How to use the LuCI app.

textfile's directory and unbound's socket also change what the jail mounts. For those, see How to publish metrics from scripts and How to monitor Unbound.

docs.title: How to Write a Collector in Your Own Package
docs.text: This guide puts a collector of yours in an OpenWrt package of your own. You test it with the exporter's devkit, and install it beside the exporter's packages. The exporter loads it as it loads its own collectors, from /usr/share/ucode/prometheus/collectors/, and holds it to the same rules.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The exporter's source, for its template: devkit/template/ in the repository or in a release's tarball.
  • An OpenWrt SDK of 25.12, to build the package, such as ghcr.io/openwrt/sdk:<arch>-25.12.<n>.
  • Somewhere to run its tests: an OpenWrt 25.12 rootfs container (ghcr.io/openwrt/rootfs:x86_64-25.12.<n>), with the packages.ucode.dev feed added, as Installing the exporter adds it.

docs.title: 1. Start from the template
docs.text:
cp -r ucode-prometheus-exporter/devkit/template my-collector
cd my-collector
File Is Makefile The OpenWrt package, ucode-prometheus-exporter-example. src/prometheus/collectors/example.uc The collector, example: seconds since boot from /proc/uptime, and each swap area from /proc/swaps. test/example_test.uc Its tests. test/fixtures/router/ What a router answered, at the paths it has there. test/utest.config.uc utest's config, on the devkit.

Rename example everywhere: the module's file, meta.name (the module's name, with - for _), the test, and PKG_NAME.

The exporter finds a collector by its file, never by its package's name. Naming the package ucode-prometheus-exporter-<name> lists it beside the exporter's packages. But a name of your own avoids a clash with a collector the exporter may add later.

docs.title: 2. Write to the collector API
docs.text:
A collector imports prometheus.exporter and nothing else. The loader leaves out a collector that imports fs or ubus, or calls require. The collector reads the system through deps, which holds the capabilities its meta.needs names.

import { Result, errors, services, proc, exposition, u32 } from 'prometheus.exporter';

Collector interface describes what the API exports, collect(deps, out, options), each capability of deps, and the recorder out. Two helpers do the most with the least code:

  • proc.rows(fs, path) returns the fields of every line of a file, [] for a blank line. It reads a table of /proc in one call, as the template reads /proc/swaps.
  • out.batch(type, rows) writes families of one sample each, without labels: [ [ name, help, value ], ... ], as the template writes the uptime.

These, and every name the API exports, are what a version of the exporter promises a collector: see About versions.

docs.title: 3. Declare what it touches
docs.text:
meta says what the collector is and what it reaches. The service builds its jail from it. The service's user is not root, and the service grants that user what the collector declares and nothing else. A path the collector does not declare is not there, and a ubus call it does not list is refused.

meta Declare The jail, from it needs The capabilities it gets in deps: fs, ubus, uci, rtnl, nl80211, socket, exec, time, log. — paths What it reads outside /proc and /sys, and the directory of each Unix socket it connects to. Mounts each, read-only. configs With uci: the uci configs it reads. Mounts each, readable by the service's group. commands With exec: the programs it runs; optional_commands, those it runs only where they are installed. Mounts each, with its libraries. ubus With ubus: { object: [ method ] }, name.* for every object under name.. Writes the service's ubus ACL. capabilities CAP_NET_ADMIN or CAP_NET_RAW, for what its reads or programs need. Grants it to the service. groups The groups whose sockets it connects to. Puts the service's user in each. proc_files With fs: the files of /proc only root reads, which it reads. Opens each to the service's group.

Collector interface gives each field's rules, and The jail what each grants. The tests below fail a collector that touches what it does not declare.

docs.title: 4. Keep the top level to declarations
docs.text:
The module's top level runs twice each time the service starts: once guarded, in a child process, and again in uhttpd's own process, from which every scrape is forked. So the top level only declares: constants, functions, meta, collect and the import. It may call ucode's functions that only compute (regexp, sprintf, map, join ...).

  • A top level that sleeps, prints, exits or loads code is left out, with COLLECTOR_IMPURE.
  • A top level that loops is left out after 5 seconds.

Put whatever the collector reads or works out in collect():

const LINE = regexp('^([a-z]+) ([0-9]+)$');   // a constant: fine

export function collect(deps, out) {
    let text = deps.fs.readfile('/proc/mine');  // reads: in collect() alone
    ...
};

The top level has the full list.

docs.title: 5. Depend on what it reads with, never on what it watches
docs.text:
In the Makefile, DEPENDS names what the collector reads WITH:

  • the exporter
  • a library (+ucode-mod-nl80211 for nl80211, +ucode-mod-socket for socket)
  • a generic program it runs (+tc, +ethtool)

Never name what it WATCHES. Installing a monitoring package must not install, and start, a daemon that changes what the router does.

Where the watched software is absent, the collector has nothing to observe: Result.none('<what> is not installed'). For a service that is installed but disabled, the API's services.unless_disabled() says so. A program that comes with the watched software (chronyc with chrony) goes in meta.optional_commands. See About nothing to observe.

docs.title: 6. Test it
docs.text:
On the test machine, install the devkit, which brings the exporter and utest:

apk add ucode-prometheus-exporter-devkit
cd my-collector
utest -c test/utest.config.uc test

with_collector runs the collector as a scrape does, with only its needs, over the mocks the test gives it. It fails the test when the collector:

  • touches a path, a socket, a program or a ubus call its meta does not declare,
  • writes text Prometheus would refuse, or
  • has a meta the loader refuses.

assert_module fails a module that the loader would leave out for its text: not strict mode, another import, or a top level that does more than declare.

import { with_collector, outcome, assert_module } from 'prometheus.exporter.devkit.collector';
import { reader } from 'prometheus.exporter.devkit.fixtures';
import * as mine from 'prometheus.collectors.mine';

const ROUTER = reader(sourcepath(0, true) + '/fixtures/router');

it('writes what the router has', () => {
    with_collector(mine, { fs: { data: ROUTER.files([ '/proc/mine' ]) } }, (r) => {
        assert.match(true, r.result.ok);
        assert.match([ '# HELP mine_value ...', ... ], r.lines);
    });
});

Capture fixtures from a device exactly as it has them:

  • a file goes at its own path under the fixtures' directory
  • a ubus reply goes in ubus/<object>.<method>.json, from ubus call <object> <method>

The devkit describes what the devkit exports, with_collector's config, the mocks for programs and rc, and the proxies' keys.

docs.title: 7. Package it
docs.text:
The template's Makefile installs the module into the collectors' directory. When the package is installed or removed, it reloads an enabled exporter, which restarts with the collector loaded or gone.

The package depends on the exporter version whose API it is written to, EXPORTER_MIN: 0.3.0, which froze the API for 1.0. From 1.0, use >=1.0.0, since only a major version breaks the API.

cp -r my-collector <sdk>/package/
cd <sdk>
make defconfig
make package/ucode-prometheus-exporter-mine/compile

The .apk is under bin/packages/<arch>/base/. Publish it in a feed of yours, or install the file directly:

apk add --allow-untrusted ucode-prometheus-exporter-mine-1.0.0-r1.apk

docs.title: 8. Check it on a device
docs.text:
The prometheus-exporter command comes in its own package, which the service does not need. Install it to check the collector:

apk add ucode-prometheus-exporter-cli
prometheus-exporter collector check /usr/share/ucode/prometheus/collectors/mine.uc
wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1:9100/metrics | grep 'collector="mine"'

collector check reads the module's text, loads it under the guards, validates its meta and runs it on the device. It fails anything the exporter would leave out or stop: see The prometheus-exporter command. node_scrape_collector_success{collector="mine"} 1 means the exporter serves it.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Collector interface, Collector contract and The devkit
  • Tutorial: write your first collector, in the exporter's own tree

docs.title: How to Monitor a Router with the Bundled Dashboards and Alerts
docs.text:
The exporter comes with alerting rules and dashboards. They are in monitoring/, in the repository and in each release's tarball:

File What it is monitoring/prometheus/exporter.rules.yml Alerts on the exporter's own health: the target down, a collector failing or quarantined, scrapes too slow for their timeout. monitoring/prometheus/router.rules.yml Alerts on a router's basics: the connection table, memory, filesystems, temperatures, the WAN, Wi-Fi radios, the clock, the DHCP pool. monitoring/prometheus/tests/ The rules' tests, for promtool test rules and vmalert-tool unittest. monitoring/grafana/ The dashboards OpenWrt router and OpenWrt exporter health, for Grafana. monitoring/perses/ The same two dashboards, for Perses.

This guide loads them into Prometheus or VictoriaMetrics, Grafana and Perses. It then says what each alert means and what to do about it.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A Prometheus, or a VictoriaMetrics with vmagent, that scrapes the router: see Monitor a router with Prometheus.
