The rules and dashboards work for every router the server scrapes, whatever you named the jobs. They find this exporter's targets by the metrics it writes, and leave other targets alone. See Which targets the alerts take.
  • The collectors whose panels and alerts you want. If a collector is not installed, its panels show no data and its alerts never fire. Nothing else breaks. See Choosing collectors.
  • A copy of monitoring/.

docs.title: 1. Load the rules into Prometheus
docs.text:
Copy the rule files where Prometheus reads its config, and name them in prometheus.yml:

rule_files:
  - /etc/prometheus/rules/openwrt/*.rules.yml

alerting:
  alertmanagers:
    - static_configs:
        - targets: [ 'alertmanager:9093' ]

No rule names a job or an instance, so the rules load unchanged, whatever you named your scrape jobs. Check the files and reload:

promtool check rules /etc/prometheus/rules/openwrt/*.rules.yml
curl -X POST http://localhost:9090/-/reload    # with --web.enable-lifecycle; or send Prometheus SIGHUP

Run Prometheus with --enable-feature=extra-scrape-metrics. With it, Prometheus writes scrape_timeout_seconds. OpenWrtExporterScrapeSlow and the Scrape duration and timeout panel compare each scrape's duration with it. Without the flag, the alert assumes Prometheus's default timeout of 10 seconds, and the panel shows only the duration.

Each alert carries severity: critical or severity: warning, for Alertmanager's routes.

docs.title: 2. Or load them into VictoriaMetrics
docs.text:
vmalert reads the same files, unchanged:

vmalert -rule='/etc/vmalert/openwrt/*.rules.yml' \
    -datasource.url=http://victoriametrics:8428 \
    -remoteWrite.url=http://victoriametrics:8428 \
    -notifier.url=http://alertmanager:9093

What differs from Prometheus:

  • vmagent writes scrape_timeout_seconds for every target, without a flag.
  • OpenWrtExporterDown looks for the exporter's ucode_prometheus_exporter_build_info over the last 7 days. MetricsQL's max_over_time, like PromQL's, ignores the staleness markers that a failed scrape writes.
  • The description of OpenWrtExporterCollectorFailing runs a query (query, sortByLabel). Both servers' templates can do this.
  • make monitoring-check also loads the rules with vmalert -dryRun and runs their tests with vmalert-tool unittest, so the rules keep working in VictoriaMetrics.
  • In Grafana and in Perses, the dashboards take VictoriaMetrics as a Prometheus data source. MetricsQL runs their PromQL.

docs.title: 3. Import the dashboards into Grafana
docs.text:
Each dashboard picks its data source, job and instance from variables at its top, so either way below imports it unchanged. The job and instance lists hold the targets that wrote the exporter's ucode_prometheus_exporter_build_info in the dashboard's time range. A node_exporter's targets are not among them.

  • By hand: Dashboards → New → Import, upload monitoring/grafana/openwrt-router.json, then exporter-health.json.

  • Provisioned: copy the two files into a directory Grafana reads, and add a provider in /etc/grafana/provisioning/dashboards/openwrt.yaml:

    apiVersion: 1
providers:
  - name: openwrt
    folder: OpenWrt
    type: file
    options:
      path: /var/lib/grafana/dashboards/openwrt

A link at the top of each dashboard opens the other one, for the same router.

docs.title: 4. Apply the dashboards to Perses
docs.text:
The dashboards take their data source from a variable. It lists the project's Prometheus data sources and the global ones, so you need one of either. Then log percli in to your Perses and apply the dashboards:

percli login https://perses.example.net
percli apply -f monitoring/perses/openwrt-router.yaml --project <project>
percli apply -f monitoring/perses/exporter-health.yaml --project <project>

To check a dashboard against your server's plugins first, run percli lint -f <file> --online.

docs.title: 5. Change a threshold
docs.text:
Each threshold is in its rule's expression. A comment above the rule says what it means. Edit the threshold there and in the rule's test in monitoring/prometheus/tests/, then run the tests:

promtool test rules monitoring/prometheus/tests/*.test.yml

In a checkout of the repository, make monitoring-check runs the tests along with every other check: see Make targets. It refuses a rule that matches a job or an instance, such as up{job="openwrt"}. To allow one, put a comment above or in the rule that says monitoring-check: allow-target-matcher and why.

docs.title: The exporter's health
docs.text:
Error codes lists the failures behind these alerts. Troubleshooting says how to find them on the router.

Alert Severity Fires when Do OpenWrtExporterDown critical up has been 0 for 5 minutes, of a target that wrote the exporter's ucode_prometheus_exporter_build_info in the last 7 days, whatever its job is called: the router or the exporter is down, the scrape timed out, or basic auth refused the scraper. A target that never answered, or that has been down for more than 7 days, does not fire it: see Which targets the alerts take. service prometheus-exporter status on the router; Prometheus's Targets page says why the scrape failed. See Prometheus cannot scrape it. OpenWrtExporterCollectorFailing warning A collector's node_scrape_collector_success has been 0 for 15 minutes: it failed, was quarantined or was left out at the deadline in every scrape. The description lists its failures since the service started, by error code. A collector with nothing to observe succeeds, and never fires it. service prometheus-exporter check runs it now and says why it fails. See A collector fails. OpenWrtExporterCollectorQuarantined warning A collector's circuit breaker tripped in the last 15 minutes: it hung, was killed, ran over its budget, had a program killed at its timeout, or failed three scrapes in a row. It is left out for 1 to 32 scrapes, then tried again. check says what tripped it, and when it is tried again. See A collector is quarantined and About deadlines and circuit breakers. OpenWrtExporterDeadlineSkips warning The scrape deadline left a collector out, or killed its program, in more than 2 scrapes of 30 minutes (SCRAPE_DEADLINE). The first scrape after a restart can be late once. The scrapes need more time than the job's scrape_timeout: scrape the slow collector in a job of its own with a longer timeout, or raise the job's. See Collectors are left out at the deadline. OpenWrtExporterProgramTimeouts warning A collector's program was killed at its timeout in the last 30 minutes (COMMAND_TIMEOUT). Give it more time, How to give programs more time, or find why the program hangs: a radio or a daemon that does not answer. OpenWrtExporterAuthFailures warning Basic auth refused more than 5 requests in 15 minutes. A scraper with the wrong password is OpenWrtExporterDown instead. A script or a scraper with an old password, or someone guessing it: keep the port to the scrapers, How to listen on the LAN. OpenWrtExporterScrapeSlow warning Scrapes took more than 80% of the scraper's timeout for 15 minutes. The exporter answers in time by leaving the slowest collectors out, so they are next. The Time in each collector panel of OpenWrt exporter health shows which collector takes the time. As for deadline skips.

docs.title: The router
docs.text: Alert Severity Fires when Do OpenWrtConntrackTableNearlyFull warning The connection table has been more than 80% full for 10 minutes. A full table drops new connections. Raise net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max, or find the host that opens them: nat_traffic's Traffic per host panel. OpenWrtMemoryLow warning Less than 10% of the memory has been available for 10 minutes. /tmp and the log are memory too. Find what grew: top, du -sh /tmp/*. OpenWrtFilesystemNearlyFull warning A writable filesystem has had less than 10% of its space available for 15 minutes. Read-only ones, as the squashfs root, are left out. On the overlay, remove packages or files; on /tmp, what fills it. OpenWrtFilesystemOutOfInodes warning A writable filesystem has had less than 10% of its inodes free for 15 minutes; one that counts none, as jffs2, is left out. Many small files: a cache or a spool that grows. OpenWrtTemperatureAboveMax warning A hwmon sensor has read at or above its chip's own maximum for 5 minutes. Some chips throttle there, as mt76's Wi-Fi radios. Check the airflow, and where the device stands. OpenWrtTemperatureCritical critical A hwmon sensor has read at or above its chip's critical temperature for a minute: the hardware may shut down. As above, now. OpenWrtThermalZoneThrottling warning A thermal zone has been at or above its passive trip point for 5 minutes: the kernel slows the CPU to cool it. As above. OpenWrtThermalZoneNearCritical critical A thermal zone has been within 10 °C of its critical trip point (node_thermal_zone_critical_celsius) for a minute: the kernel shuts the router down at it. As above, at once: a fan stopped, a vent blocked, a router in the sun. OpenWrtWanDown critical The logical interface wan has been down for 5 minutes. Name yours in the expression: wan\|wan6, wwan. ifstatus wan on the router; node_openwrt_interface_errors counts the errors netifd holds for it. OpenWrtWifiRadioDown warning A Wi-Fi radio the wireless config enables has had no network up for 10 minutes (node_wifi_radio_up); one disabled on purpose (node_wifi_radio_disabled) is left out. wifi status on the router: its driver or hostapd failed, or none of its networks is enabled. OpenWrtClockNotSynchronized warning The NTP daemon has not had the clock synchronized for 30 minutes. No NTP server answers, or none is set: System → System → Time Synchronization in LuCI. OpenWrtDhcpPoolNearlyExhausted warning An interface has had 90% or more of its DHCPv4 pool leased for 15 minutes: dnsmasq's and odhcpd's leases over node_openwrt_dhcp_pool_size, which dhcp_leases works out from the interface's start and limit in /etc/config/dhcp and its subnet. Raise the interface's limit in /etc/config/dhcp, or shorten its leasetime.

docs.title: Which targets the alerts take
docs.text:
No rule names a job or an instance. Instead, each rule takes the targets that write ucode_prometheus_exporter_build_info. Only this exporter writes it, and every scrape has it, whatever collect[] selects. So:

  • The rules load unchanged, whatever you named the scrape jobs.
  • A Linux server's node_exporter in the same Prometheus fires none of them, even though it also writes node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes or node_scrape_collector_success.

OpenWrtExporterDown cannot look at the current ucode_prometheus_exporter_build_info. A target that does not answer writes nothing, and its series went stale with the failed scrape. So the alert looks over the last 7 days instead, with max_over_time(ucode_prometheus_exporter_build_info[7d]). It fires for a target that is down and wrote the metric in that time:

  • 7 days means a router that is down over a weekend, or while you are away for a week, still alerts when someone looks. After 7 days, the alert no longer knows the target as this exporter's and resolves, even though the router is still down. Each evaluation reads 7 days of one series per target: 10,080 samples at one scrape a minute. If Prometheus keeps less than 7 days, the alert looks back as far as Prometheus keeps.
  • A target that never answered never wrote the metric. This happens when you add a target with a wrong address, port or password. The alert cannot tell it from another exporter's target, so it does not fire. When you add a router, check the Targets page of Prometheus, or of vmagent.
  • A target removed from the scrape config has no up at all, so it fires nothing, as in any Prometheus.

To alert on a job's targets whatever they run, keep a rule of your own: up{job="<your job>"} == 0.

docs.title: OpenWrt router
docs.text:
This dashboard shows a router or an access point. At the top are its uptime, clock, load and release. Below them are panels for:

  • CPU and load, and memory
  • the network devices' traffic, errors and drops, and the logical interfaces
  • the Wi-Fi clients, their signal, and the channels' use
  • the connection table and the traffic per host
  • the temperatures
  • the filesystems' space and inodes
  • the DHCP leases
  • the WireGuard peers' handshakes and traffic
  • the clock's offset
GrafanaPerses

The lab (make lab) has no Wi-Fi radio, no WireGuard interface and no firewall. Those panels show no data there, as on a router without those collectors.

docs.title: OpenWrt exporter health
docs.text:
This dashboard shows the exporter itself:

  • whether its scrapes succeed, and its version
  • how many collectors fail or are quarantined
  • each scrape's duration against the scraper's timeout, and the time spent in each collector
  • each collector's success, samples, and failures by error code
  • the circuit breakers and the deadline
  • the memory, CPU and file descriptors of the uhttpd instance that serves the scrapes

The counters come from the exporter collector, in the base package. They restart at 0 when the service restarts.

GrafanaPerses

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Metrics lists every family the dashboards and alerts use. make monitoring-check fails on a family that is not there.
  • About deadlines and circuit breakers
  • Pushing metrics from the router, where nothing can scrape it.

docs.title: How to Give Programs More Time
docs.text:
Some collectors run programs: ethtool, nft, tc, chronyc, mmcli, ubnt-manager. By default, a collector's programs get 5 seconds in all per scrape. If a program is still running after that, the exporter kills it, and the collector fails with COMMAND_TIMEOUT.

Give the programs more time when a slow device, or a slow radio over ssh, needs it. Give them less to keep a scrape short.

docs.title: Find the collector that runs out of time
docs.text:
Browser (LuCI)Terminal (SSH)

Open Status → System Log, and look for COMMAND_TIMEOUT on the lines with prometheus-exporter. Status → Prometheus exporter also shows a collector that failed its test run with this code under Test run.

logread -e prometheus-exporter | grep COMMAND_TIMEOUT

The log line looks like this:

daemon.warn prometheus-exporter[1]: collector 'ubnt-manager': COMMAND_TIMEOUT (ubnt-manager: still running after 5 s, killed)

Over SSH, service prometheus-exporter check shows each collector's timeout and where it comes from:

  ubnt-manager (Ubiquiti airOS radios): section 'ubnt_manager', enabled
      timeout  5s # the main section's exec_timeout

docs.title: Give one collector more time
docs.text:
The collector's timeout takes 1 to 30 seconds.

Browser (LuCI)Terminal (SSH)
  1. On Services → Prometheus exporter, tab Collectors, press Edit on the collector's row.
  2. Set Program timeout, such as 10, and press Save.
  3. Press Save & Apply.

Set timeout in the collector's section. The section is named after its module (ubnt_manager for ubnt-manager):

uci set prometheus-exporter.ubnt_manager=collector
uci set prometheus-exporter.ubnt_manager.timeout=10
uci commit prometheus-exporter
service prometheus-exporter reload

docs.title: Change the default for every collector
docs.text:
The default takes 1 to 30 seconds. It applies to every collector that sets no timeout of its own.

Browser (LuCI)Terminal (SSH)

On Services → Prometheus exporter, tab Limits, set Program timeout, such as 3, and press Save & Apply.

Set exec_timeout in the main section:

uci set prometheus-exporter.main.exec_timeout=3
uci commit prometheus-exporter
service prometheus-exporter reload

docs.title: Keep within Prometheus's timeout
docs.text:
The collectors run one after the other, so a scrape can take as long as all their programs' timeouts added up, and more. Prometheus gives a scrape scrape_timeout, 10 seconds by default, and drops the whole scrape when it runs out. If you raise a collector's timeout close to that, also raise scrape_timeout for that job, or scrape that collector in a job of its own:

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: openwrt-radios
    scrape_interval: 60s
    scrape_timeout: 30s
    params:
      collect[]: [ ubnt-manager ]
    static_configs:
      - targets: [ 'router.lan:9100' ]

Then leave it out of the main job with exclude[]: [ ubnt-manager ].

Collector interface has the rules for the timeouts, and UCI configuration the options.

docs.title: How to Compress Scrapes
docs.text: The exporter gzips a scrape when the scraper asks for it with Accept-Encoding: gzip. Prometheus and vmagent send that header by default. Compression is on unless you turned it off.

docs.title: Check that scrapes are compressed
docs.text:
curl -s -o /dev/null -D - -H 'Accept-Encoding: gzip' http://router.lan:9100/metrics

A compressed reply has Content-Encoding: gzip. While compression is on, service prometheus-exporter status says gzip when asked, and LuCI's Status → Prometheus exporter says Compression: gzip, when the scraper asks for it.

docs.title: Turn it off
docs.text:
Turn it off if the scraper's CPU, or the router's, matters more than the bytes on the network:

Browser (LuCI)Terminal (SSH)

On Services → Prometheus exporter, tab General, untick Compress, and press Save & Apply.

uci set prometheus-exporter.main.compress=0
uci commit prometheus-exporter
service prometheus-exporter reload

Scrapes are then plain text, whatever the scraper asks for.

docs.title: Turn it back on
docs.text:
Browser (LuCI)Terminal (SSH)

On Services → Prometheus exporter, tab General, tick Compress, and press Save & Apply.

uci set prometheus-exporter.main.compress=1
uci commit prometheus-exporter
service prometheus-exporter reload

docs.title: For one scraper only
docs.text:
Leave compress on, and make the scraper that wants plain text stop asking for gzip. In Prometheus 2.49 and later, set enable_compression: false in its scrape config. The exporter also answers plain text to a request with Accept-Encoding: gzip;q=0.

Performance on small routers says what a compressed scrape saves and costs. HTTP endpoint has the rules of the reply.

docs.title: How to Serve HTTPS with Basic Auth
docs.text:
Make every scrape log in with a user and password, over TLS. The exporter accepts basic auth only over HTTPS. Set the certificate and key along with it, or the service refuses the configuration.

flowchart LR
    P[Prometheus] -- "HTTPS, user and password" --> U["uhttpd, port 9100<br/>TLS with cert and key"]
    U --> H{"the handler: do they match<br/>auth_user and the hash?"}
    H -- yes --> M[the scrape]
    H -- no --> R[401 Unauthorized]

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A TLS library for uhttpd: ls /lib/libustream-ssl.so finds it. If it is missing, install one, such as apk add libustream-mbedtls.

  • A certificate and its key, for the name Prometheus uses to reach the device. Each must be a file of at most 64 KiB under /etc/ssl, /etc/acme or /etc/prometheus-exporter, or uhttpd's own /etc/uhttpd.*. The service copies no other files (see About the security model). To make a self-signed certificate for router.lan:

    mkdir -p /etc/prometheus-exporter
px5g selfsigned -days 3650 -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 \
    -keyout /etc/prometheus-exporter/tls.key -out /etc/prometheus-exporter/tls.crt \
    -subj /CN=router.lan -addext subjectAltName=DNS:router.lan

    uhttpd's own /etc/uhttpd.crt and /etc/uhttpd.key also work. But they name OpenWrt unless uhttpd's config says otherwise, and the certificate is DER. Convert it to PEM for Prometheus (openssl x509 -inform der -in uhttpd.crt -out openwrt.crt).

docs.title: 1. Save the password's hash
docs.text:
Use a long random password: a scraper does not need to remember it. The configuration holds the password's crypt hash, never the password. The hash lives in its own config, /etc/config/prometheus-exporter-auth, apart from the rest of the configuration, which LuCI's settings page may read.

Have the exporter hash the password and save the hash there, so the password appears on no command line of the device:

Browser (LuCI)Terminal (SSH)
  1. Open Services → Prometheus exporter, tab HTTPS & login.
  2. Fill in TLS certificate and TLS key with the files of the prerequisites, such as /etc/prometheus-exporter/tls.crt and /etc/prometheus-exporter/tls.key. Change password… needs them.

  3. Press Change password…, type the password in New password and again in Confirmation, and press Change password.

The hash is saved at once, separately from Save & Apply. See How to use the LuCI app.

ubus call prometheus-exporter set_password '{"password":"…"}'

{
    "saved": true
}

Or save a hash yourself, over SSH. prometheus-exporter hash-password (in the command line's package, ucode-prometheus-exporter-cli) reads the password without echoing it, and prints the hash:

uci set prometheus-exporter-auth.main.auth_password="$(prometheus-exporter hash-password)"
uci commit prometheus-exporter-auth

A hash made elsewhere must be one of these:

  • $1$, as uhttpd -m <password> prints
  • $5$ or $6$ of at most 2000 rounds, as mkpasswd -m sha-512 -R 1000 makes

openssl passwd -6 makes hashes of 5000 rounds, which the service refuses. Performance on small routers says why. When you set a hash by hand, put it in single quotes, or the shell reads its $.

The service does not accept:

  • A DES-crypt hash. Its 13 characters could be a plain password, which uhttpd compares as text when it does not start with $.
  • bcrypt, which ucode cannot compute in the time of a scrape.

A hash made elsewhere must also write rounds= as musl writes it back: without a leading zero, and in range. Otherwise no password matches it.

docs.title: 2. Set the user, and HTTPS
docs.text:
Browser (LuCI)Terminal (SSH)
  1. On the same HTTPS & login tab, check that TLS certificate and TLS key are filled in.
  2. Type the user in Basic auth user, such as prometheus.
  3. Press Save & Apply.
uci set prometheus-exporter.main.auth_user='prometheus'
uci set prometheus-exporter.main.cert='/etc/prometheus-exporter/tls.crt'
uci set prometheus-exporter.main.key='/etc/prometheus-exporter/tls.key'
uci commit prometheus-exporter
service prometheus-exporter reload

Basic auth is on while auth_user is set. If the service refuses the configuration, LuCI's Save error dialog or logread -e prometheus-exporter says why. The reasons are:

  • a user without a saved hash
  • a hash the service does not accept
  • no cert and key
  • cert or key outside those directories (TLS_PATH)
  • cert or key not a regular file of at most 64 KiB, or a link out of those directories (TLS_FILE)

docs.title: 3. Check it
docs.text:
Browser (LuCI)Terminal (SSH)

Open Status → Prometheus exporter. Under Service, Metrics gives an https:// address, and Basic auth says A scrape logs in, over HTTPS.

service prometheus-exporter status

running
listening on https://192.168.1.1:9100/metrics, basic auth, gzip when asked, serving 16 collectors

From the machine that scrapes:

curl -sk -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://router.lan:9100/metrics
curl -sk -u prometheus:'…' https://router.lan:9100/metrics | head

The first command prints 401. The second prints the scrape.

docs.title: 4. Scrape it
docs.text:
In Prometheus, or in vmagent, which takes the same scrape_configs:

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: openwrt
    scheme: https
    basic_auth:
      username: prometheus
      password_file: /etc/prometheus/openwrt.password
    tls_config:
      ca_file: /etc/prometheus/openwrt.crt   # the router's certificate, self-signed
      server_name: router.lan                # a name the certificate holds
      # insecure_skip_verify: true           # or: no check of the certificate at all
    static_configs:
      - targets: [ 'router.lan:9100' ]

Copy the router's certificate (/etc/prometheus-exporter/tls.crt), not its key, to the Prometheus host as ca_file.

docs.title: Renew the certificate
docs.text:
The service's jail holds the certificate and key it started with. After you write new ones at the same paths, reload the service. It restarts with the new files:

service prometheus-exporter reload

A tool that renews certificates on its own, such as acme, runs that reload from its hook. Until the reload, the service serves the old certificate. OpenWrt's acme keeps certificates in /etc/ssl/acme, and acme.sh's own in /etc/acme. cert and key may point there, and so may their links.

docs.title: Turn it off
docs.text:
Browser (LuCI)Terminal (SSH)
  1. On the HTTPS & login tab, empty Basic auth user, and press Save & Apply.
  2. Press Remove password, then Remove password in the dialog.
uci delete prometheus-exporter.main.auth_user
uci commit prometheus-exporter
ubus call prometheus-exporter set_password '{"password":""}'
service prometheus-exporter reload

The empty password removes the saved hash.

Without a user, a saved hash would go unused anyway.

If cert and key are still set, the exporter serves HTTPS without a login. To serve HTTP, delete them too.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• HTTP endpoint: the replies.
  • About the security model: why HTTPS only, and why the handler checks the password itself.
  • In LuCI, Change password… on the HTTPS & login tab hashes the password for you, and saves the hash at once. See How to use the LuCI app.

docs.title: How to Install the Exporter
docs.text: Add the exporter's feed, install the base package, then install the collectors you want, one by one or in groups. The service starts on its own, on loopback, port 9100.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A device on OpenWrt 25.12, with a shell on it (ssh), that can reach the internet.
  • Neither prometheus-node-exporter-ucode nor prometheus-node-exporter-lua is installed. If one is, see How to move from the feed's exporters instead.

docs.title: 1. Add the feed
docs.text:
This step needs a shell on the device: LuCI's System → Software page cannot add a signing key.

The exporter's packages are in the packages.ucode.dev feed. So is ucode-docopt, which the command line's package depends on and OpenWrt's own feeds lack. The base package's dependencies (uhttpd, ucode modules and rpcd-mod-ucode) come from the release's own feeds. Add the feed and its signing key:

feed=https://m00qek.github.io/packages.ucode.dev/25.12
wget -qO /etc/apk/keys/packages.ucode.dev.pem "$feed/feed.pub.pem"
echo "$feed" > /etc/apk/repositories.d/ucode-dev.list
apk update

apk then checks every package of the feed against that key, as it checks OpenWrt's packages against the release's key.

docs.title: 2. Choose the packages
docs.text:
• ucode-prometheus-exporter, the base package: the service and the collectors every device can use.
  • A collector's package, ucode-prometheus-exporter-<name>, for each other collector you want: -wifi, -dnsmasq, -wireguard.
  • Or a group: -network, -wireless, -hardware, or -full for all three and the services every router has.
  • luci-app-prometheus-exporter, for its pages in LuCI.
  • ucode-prometheus-exporter-cli, for the prometheus-exporter command. It prints a scrape on standard output, hashes a password, and checks a collector before you install it. The service and LuCI do not need it. On a router short of flash, leave it out (see How to run the exporter on a small device).

Collectors lists every collector, its package and its groups.

docs.title: 3. Install them
docs.text:
From the feed:

Browser (LuCI)Terminal (SSH)
  1. Open System → Software and press Update lists….
  2. Type prometheus-exporter in Filter.
  3. On the Available tab, press Install… on the row of ucode-prometheus-exporter, then Install in the dialog.
  4. Do the same for each other package you chose: ucode-prometheus-exporter-full, luci-app-prometheus-exporter, ucode-prometheus-exporter-cli.
  5. Reload the browser page, so LuCI shows the app's pages.
apk update
apk add ucode-prometheus-exporter ucode-prometheus-exporter-full luci-app-prometheus-exporter ucode-prometheus-exporter-cli

Or from .apk files, over SSH. make package builds them into bin/ (see Make targets). Copy them to the device's /tmp, and set version to the files' version, as their names end:

version=0.3.0-r1
apk update
apk add --allow-untrusted /tmp/ucode-prometheus-exporter-$version.apk \
    /tmp/ucode-prometheus-exporter-wifi-$version.apk \
    /tmp/luci-app-prometheus-exporter-$version.apk

The command line's file, ucode-prometheus-exporter-cli-$version.apk, also needs ucode-docopt. apk takes it from the feed of step 1, unless you add its file too.

A group's file brings nothing without its collectors' files, so install them together. Every package must have the same version as the base package.

docs.title: 4. Check that it serves
docs.text:
Browser (LuCI)Terminal (SSH)

Open Status → Prometheus exporter. Under Service, State says Running, and Metrics gives the address it serves, http://127.0.0.1:9100/metrics (reachable from the router only). Under Collectors, Test run says what each collector found.

service prometheus-exporter status
wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1:9100/metrics | head

status says where the exporter listens and how many collectors it serves. To see what each collector found, run service prometheus-exporter check.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• How to listen on the LAN, for a Prometheus elsewhere.
  • How to serve HTTPS with basic auth.
  • How to choose collectors.

docs.title: How to Listen on the LAN
docs.text: By default, the exporter listens on loopback, so only programs on the device reach it. To scrape it from another machine, make it listen on an interface that machine reaches.

docs.title: 1. Choose the interface
docs.text:
Use the name of a logical interface, as /etc/config/network and LuCI name it (lan), not the name of a device (br-lan). LuCI's Listen on lists them, and so does ubus call prometheus-exporter interfaces.

*, which LuCI shows as Every address, listens on every address of the device, including the WAN's. Prefer one interface.

docs.title: 2. Set it
docs.text:
Browser (LuCI)Terminal (SSH)
  1. Open Services → Prometheus exporter, tab General.
  2. Pick the interface in Listen on, such as lan. To change the port too, set Port.
  3. Press Save & Apply.
uci set prometheus-exporter.main.listen_interface=lan
uci commit prometheus-exporter
service prometheus-exporter reload

To change the port too, set listen_port.

The service listens on every IPv4 and IPv6 address of the interface. While the interface has no address, the service does not start. It logs deferring start until listen interface lan becomes ready, and starts once the interface comes up. It restarts whenever the interface goes down and up again.

docs.title: 3. Check it
docs.text:
On the device:

Browser (LuCI)Terminal (SSH)

Open Status → Prometheus exporter. Under Service, Metrics lists each address the exporter serves, such as http://192.168.1.1:9100/metrics.

service prometheus-exporter status

running
listening on http://192.168.1.1:9100/metrics, http://[fd00:ab:cd::1]:9100/metrics, gzip when asked, serving 16 collectors

From the machine that will scrape it:

curl -s http://192.168.1.1:9100/metrics | head

docs.title: If it does not answer
docs.text:
• The firewall must accept input on the port from that zone. OpenWrt's default lan zone accepts input. Another zone may need a rule:

    uci add firewall rule
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].name='Allow-Prometheus'
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].src='lan'
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].dest_port='9100'
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].proto='tcp'
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].target='ACCEPT'
uci commit firewall
service firewall reload

    Never open the port from wan: the metrics name your devices, addresses and clients.

  • If status does not say running (in LuCI, State is not Running), the interface has no address yet, and the service is waiting for one. Check ifstatus lan.

docs.title: Keep it to the scrapers
docs.text:
Every request to /metrics is a scrape, which keeps the router's CPU busy for a while. With basic auth, each request also costs a password check, which is more expensive. uhttpd runs 3 requests at once and makes the rest wait (see HTTP endpoint). So anyone who reaches the port can delay Prometheus's scrapes.

Let only the scrapers reach the port. Add a rule that accepts the port from the Prometheus host alone, before the zone's own policy, and a rule that rejects it for the rest of the zone:

uci add firewall rule
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].name='Allow-Prometheus'
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].src='lan'
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].src_ip='192.168.1.10'
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].dest_port='9100'
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].proto='tcp'
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].target='ACCEPT'
uci add firewall rule
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].name='Deny-Prometheus-others'
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].src='lan'
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].dest_port='9100'
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].proto='tcp'
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].target='REJECT'
uci commit firewall
service firewall reload

Replace 192.168.1.10 with the Prometheus host's address. fw4 matches rules in order, so the first rule lets the Prometheus host in and the second keeps the rest of the LAN out.

To require a password for every scrape, sent over TLS, see How to serve HTTPS with basic auth.

docs.title: How to Use the LuCI App
docs.text: luci-app-prometheus-exporter lets you set up the exporter from LuCI, and see how it is doing.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • luci-app-prometheus-exporter is installed, at the same version as the base package. After installing it, reload LuCI in the browser.

docs.title: Change the exporter's settings
docs.text:
1. Open Services → Prometheus exporter. The settings are on three tabs:
    • General: whether it runs, where it listens, keep-alive, compression and zero values;
    • HTTPS & login: the TLS certificate and key, and basic auth;
    • Limits: the seconds programs, a scrape and a collector get.

  2. Change the fields. As you type, the form marks a value the exporter would not take, and says why. A tab with such fields shows how many in its title.

  3. Press Save & Apply. If the exporter would refuse a value, nothing is saved. A Save error dialog lists each problem and why, with each field under its tab. Press a field's name to go to it, fix it, and save again.

To serve the LAN, pick its interface in Listen on, on General.

Basic auth needs HTTPS. On HTTPS & login, fill in TLS certificate and TLS key first, then Basic auth user, and press Save & Apply. The password is not a field of the form, and Save, Save & Apply and Revert do not touch it. As with LuCI's own router password, you change it separately, and the change applies at once.

docs.title: Change basic auth's password
docs.text:
1. On HTTPS & login, Basic auth password says whether a password is saved: Set or Not set. Press Change password…. It needs TLS certificate and TLS key filled in.
  2. Type the new password in New password and again in Confirmation, and press Change password.
  3. The hash is saved at once, and the exporter reloads with it. Give every scraper the new password. The password itself is never stored, and the page never sees the hash.

To turn basic auth off, empty Basic auth user and press Save & Apply. A saved password is then unused. Once the user is empty, Remove password also removes the password. Like a change, the removal applies at once.

docs.title: Switch a collector off or on
docs.text:
1. Open the Collectors tab. It lists the collectors by title, and above them, how many are switched on.

    2. Untick the collector to stop serving its metrics, or tick it to serve them again. 3. Press Save & Apply.

docs.title: Set a collector's options
docs.text:
1. On the Collectors tab, press Edit on the collector's row. The dialog shows the collector's options, and, if it runs programs, the seconds they get. Below them, it shows what the collector reads and runs, and what its jail mounts.
  2. Change the fields, and press Save. The values are staged, not applied: they show among LuCI's unsaved changes.
  3. Press Save & Apply on the page.

Dismiss, or Escape, drops the dialog's changes.

docs.title: See how the exporter does
docs.text:
1. Open Status → Prometheus exporter. The page runs each enabled collector once on the router, as a test run. It shows:

    • A banner above the tables, for what needs attention: the exporter is enabled but not running, collectors failed, or the service quarantined collectors.
    • Whether the service runs, is enabled and starts at boot, and where it serves /metrics.
    • Each collector, failed ones first. Test run says OK, Failed with why and its error code, Nothing to observe with why, or Not run: switched off. Service's scrapes says whether the service quarantined the collector, or its deadline left the collector out lately.

    2. If the banner says the exporter is enabled but not running, press System → Startup to start it, or System log to see why it stopped. 3. If a collector failed, its error code links to what the code means. See How to troubleshoot. 4. Refresh runs the test run again.

The test run is not one of the service's scrapes. It is a scrape of its own, in a jail like the service's and with the same deadline, so its results can differ from what Prometheus gets. If a collector is OK in Test run but fails in Prometheus, the service quarantined it or left it out, as Service's scrapes says. See How to troubleshoot.

docs.title: If a page says the ubus object is not available
docs.text: The pages talk to the exporter through its ubus object, which rpcd serves. The object is missing while rpcd reloads, or while the package is being upgraded. The pages then say so, and the settings are read-only. Reload the page in a moment. If the message stays, check that rpcd runs and loaded the object: ubus list prometheus-exporter.

docs.title: Let another user in
docs.text: The app's ACL is luci-app-prometheus-exporter. A LuCI user granted it can read and write /etc/config/prometheus-exporter and call the exporter's ubus object, and nothing else. With read access alone, the user sees the pages and a collector's options under Edit, but cannot save. See LuCI app.

docs.title: How to Move from the Feed's Exporters
docs.text: This exporter replaces the packages feed's prometheus-node-exporter-ucode and prometheus-node-exporter-lua. It conflicts with both, takes over their settings when you install it, and writes different metric names. Migrate from prometheus-node-exporter-lua/-ucode lists every package and family of theirs, and this exporter's equivalent of each.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
1. Note the collector packages installed: apk info | grep prometheus-node-exporter. Each has a package here: Packages.
  2. Find the queries, alerts, recording rules and dashboards that use the old names. Metric families says what each name is now, and PromQL how the common queries read.
  3. If your fleet moves router by router, add the transition's relabeling to the job of the routers still on a feed exporter.
  4. Remove the old exporter and install this one: steps 1 and 2 below.
  5. Check what the install took over, and run service prometheus-exporter check: step 3. If a collector section from the ucode exporter has a value this exporter refuses, the service does not start.
  6. Install the collector packages of step 1, or a group: apk add ucode-prometheus-exporter-full.
  7. Point Prometheus at the new port if it changed, and update the queries: step 4.
  8. Load the bundled alerts and dashboards, if you want them: How to monitor a router with the bundled dashboards and alerts.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• One of the feed's exporters is installed, with its collector packages.
  • The device has the exporter's feed: see How to install the exporter.

docs.title: 1. Remove the old exporter
docs.text:
apk does not install this exporter beside either feed exporter, or the other way round, and says why:

ERROR: unable to select packages:
  prometheus-node-exporter-ucode-2024.02.07-r2:
    breaks: ucode-prometheus-exporter-0.2.0-r1[!prometheus-node-exporter-ucode>=0]

Remove the old exporter and its collector packages first:

apk del -r prometheus-node-exporter-ucode

or prometheus-node-exporter-lua. If you changed the old config file, apk keeps it. The next step reads it.

docs.title: 2. Install this exporter
docs.text:
apk add ucode-prometheus-exporter ucode-prometheus-exporter-full

When the package is installed, its uci-defaults script copies the old config's settings into /etc/config/prometheus-exporter, once:

  • From the main section: listen_interface, listen_port, http_keepalive, cert, key and omit_zero_values.
  • From the ucode exporter: each named config collector section, with each option the collector takes (wifi's stations). It skips a collector this exporter does not have, and the log names it.
  • When both old configs are there, it takes the ucode exporter's.

It does this only while /etc/config/prometheus-exporter is as the package ships it. The script writes a valid configuration:

  • A port left at the old exporter's default (the ucode one's 9101) becomes 9100. A port you chose is kept.
  • A value this exporter would refuse is left at its default, and the script logs it.
  • An option a collector does not have is left out, and the script logs it.

The script checks a collector section's options as the service checks them, against the installed collector. But the script runs while the base package installs, before the packages installed with it. So it checks a collector that is not installed yet against two things: what the feed's ucode exporter had for it (wifi's stations), and the options every collector has (enabled, budget, max_samples).

The old config file stays as it was. The configuration lists what is not taken over.

docs.title: 3. Check what it took
docs.text:
logread -e prometheus-exporter | grep -e imported -e 'left at' -e 'left out' -e 'nothing imported'
uci show prometheus-exporter
service prometheus-exporter check

The log names every option the script took, every value it left at the default, and every option it left out, and why. See Log messages.

docs.title: 4. Update Prometheus
docs.text:
• The port. If the old exporter was the ucode one on 9101, scrape 9100, or set listen_port back to 9101.
  • The metric names. They differ from the old exporters'. Most follow node_exporter. Migrate from prometheus-node-exporter-lua/-ucode lists every family, and Renamed metrics says why each changed. Update the queries, alerts and recording rules that use an old name. Dashboards made for node_exporter work unchanged.
  • The collectors. A query that selected collectors with collect[]= still works, and so does collect=, the ucode exporter's spelling.
  • The Lua exporter's wifi_stations. This exporter has no such collector. Install ucode-prometheus-exporter-wifi: its option stations, on by default, writes the station metrics. The exporter refuses collect[]=wifi_stations, so select wifi.
  • WireGuard peer names. The old exporters always labelled peers with their description. This one does so only after uci set prometheus-exporter.wireguard=collector; uci set prometheus-exporter.wireguard.peer_names=1; uci commit prometheus-exporter; service prometheus-exporter reload. See Security model for why it is off.

docs.title: If nothing was imported
docs.text: /etc/config/prometheus-exporter is not as the package ships it: nothing imported from /etc/config/<old> means the new config was already changed. Set the options by hand: see UCI configuration.

docs.title: How to Push Metrics from the Router
docs.text: Sometimes nothing can reach the router to scrape it: it is behind NAT, or on a link that comes and goes. The router can then send its metrics instead. Cron runs prometheus-exporter scrape and posts the scrape to a Prometheus Pushgateway, or to VictoriaMetrics' import endpoint.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The exporter installed, with the collectors you want, and its command line, ucode-prometheus-exporter-cli: see How to install the exporter. The service itself need not run. If nothing scrapes it, run service prometheus-exporter disable.
  • curl: apk add curl.
  • A Pushgateway or VictoriaMetrics the router can reach.

docs.title: 1. Write the script
docs.text:
#!/bin/sh
# /usr/bin/push-metrics: a scrape of the router, posted to $URL.
URL='http://vm.lan:8428/api/v1/import/prometheus?extra_label=instance=router'
out=$(mktemp) || exit 1
trap 'rm -f "$out"' EXIT
prometheus-exporter scrape >"$out" || exit 1
curl -fsS --max-time 10 --data-binary @"$out" "$URL"

The script posts only a whole scrape. If the command refuses the scrape (for example, because it names a collector that is not installed), it exits 1 and the script posts nothing.

For a Pushgateway, post to its grouping key instead:

URL='http://pushgateway.lan:9091/metrics/job/openwrt/instance/router'

To push only some collectors, name them: prometheus-exporter scrape cpu meminfo netdev.

docs.title: 2. Run it from cron
docs.text:
chmod +x /usr/bin/push-metrics
echo '* * * * * /usr/bin/push-metrics' >>/etc/crontabs/root
service cron restart

This runs the script once a minute. Each run takes at most the main section's scrape_timeout, 10 seconds by default, whatever a collector does.

docs.title: 3. Check it
docs.text:
/usr/bin/push-metrics && echo pushed
logread -e prometheus-exporter

A collector that failed shows in the log, and in the scrape itself as node_scrape_collector_success 0.

docs.title: What differs from a scrape of /metrics
docs.text:
• The same collectors, the same rules. The command runs the collectors as the service does: each in its own process, stopped at its budget, limited to its max_samples, and in the service's jail where ujail can run (see The prometheus-exporter command).
  • No ledger. Each run is a separate process, so nothing stays quarantined from one run to the next, and the collectors run in the order of their names. A collector that keeps failing costs every run its budget: disable it.
  • No exporter counters. ucode_prometheus_exporter_*_total count the service's scrapes, and a push makes none.
  • Timestamps. The Pushgateway refuses a sample with a timestamp, and a textfile *.prom file may have one. Leave such files out of a push to the Pushgateway.
  • up and scrape_duration_seconds come from Prometheus, for a scrape it made, so a pushed series has neither. Alert on the series going stale instead.

docs.title: How to Run the Exporter on a Small Device
docs.text:
On a router with 32 or 64 MB of RAM and 4 to 16 MB of flash:

  • install the base package alone,
  • add only the collectors you need, and
  • leave out the command line and the LuCI app where flash is short.

The figures below were measured on QEMU's MIPS 24Kc (make bench-qemu, 32-bit, like MT7621-class and ath79-class routers) and on a Cortex-A53 access point.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• OpenWrt 25.12, with the exporter's feed added: see How to install the exporter.
  • The device's free flash and RAM: df -h /overlay and free.

docs.title: 1. Check what it takes
docs.text:
Flash. The table gives installed sizes as apk counts them, uncompressed. On a JFFS2 overlay, which compresses with LZMA, the base package takes about 120 KiB. The packages install their code without comments.

Package Installed ucode-prometheus-exporter, the base package 264 KiB what it needs besides, on an image with LuCI uhttpd-mod-ucode and ucode-mod-zlib, 12 KiB each (mipsel) what it needs besides, on an image without LuCI uhttpd, uhttpd-mod-ucode, rpcd-mod-ucode, ucode-mod-uloop, -zlib, -digest and -log: some 200 KiB (x86_64's sizes) a collector's package 1 to 12 KiB ucode-prometheus-exporter-cli, the command line, and ucode-docopt 10 and 43 KiB luci-app-prometheus-exporter 54 KiB

Take a 1.6 MB JFFS2 overlay (26 blocks of 64 KiB, LZMA), like a small access point's rootfs_data, empty apart from what these packages install. The base package, the LuCI app and three collectors (-wifi, -hostapd_stations, -thermal) take 296 KiB of it, apk's database included, and leave room for 1,092 KiB more. Upgrading them in place writes each new file beside the old one, and needs 20 KiB more. This was measured on QEMU's malta with an mtdram device. Your overlay's other files come on top, so check df /overlay first.

ucode, ucode-mod-fs, -ubus, -uci and -rtnl are in every 25.12 image with Wi-Fi. In the -full group, the programs that ethtool and qdisc run take more flash than all the group's collectors together: ethtool is 72 KiB, and tc-tiny and kmod-sched-core are 279 and 172 KiB.

RAM. uhttpd holds the handler and its collectors for as long as it runs. On the 24Kc, they take about 1.0 MB with the base collectors, or 1.5 MB with every collector of the -full group, on top of uhttpd's own memory. A scrape forks a process, which forks the collectors' child process. For the scrape's duration, they take about 2 MB more with the base collectors, or 4.5 MB with every collector. In a 64 MB QEMU guest with the base package, the -full group and the command line installed, the service served all 36 collectors. Its uhttpd held 1.7 MB (RssAnon), and the guest had 14.6 MB available.

memory_limit. Each of the exporter's processes may use memory_limit MB of data. The default, 0, means a quarter of the RAM, at most 64. On the 24Kc, the handler loads and a scrape succeeds with as little as 3 MB with the base collectors, or 5 MB with every collector (7 MB on a 64-bit CPU). A quarter of a 32 MB router's RAM, about 6 MB, is enough for either. A 64 MB router gets about 13 MB. See memory_limit's floor.

docs.title: 2. Install the base package alone
docs.text:
apk update
apk add ucode-prometheus-exporter

The exporter serves without the command line or the LuCI app. service prometheus-exporter check checks the configuration without the command, and uci sets it. Add ucode-prometheus-exporter-cli only if you push metrics from cron or check a collector. Add luci-app-prometheus-exporter only if the device has LuCI.

docs.title: 3. Add only the collectors you need
docs.text:
Install collectors one by one rather than as a group. The -full group brings ethtool and tc, and the collectors that cost the most on a slow CPU. What each collector costs gives each collector's memory at rest and cost per scrape, on the 24Kc and the A53. On a small router:

  • 32 MB of RAM, 4 MB of flash: the base collectors. Disable those you do not use (see How to choose collectors). The exporter neither holds nor runs a disabled collector.
  • 64 MB of RAM, 8 MB of flash: add what the device has: -wifi on an access point, -netstat, -openwrt, -wireguard, and -thermal or -hwmon where it has sensors.
  • Leave out:
    • nat_traffic on a router with a large connection table (5.6 s for 20,000 connections on the 24Kc)
    • ethtool (1.4 s on the benchmark's 17 ports on the 24Kc, plus its program's flash)
    • dhcp_leases where there are thousands of leases
    • hostapd_stations where wifi with stations does the job
    • qdisc without SQM
    • unbound unless you run Unbound. A scrape parses Unbound's statistics, which takes 30 ms on the 24Kc.
apk add ucode-prometheus-exporter-wifi ucode-prometheus-exporter-netstat

docs.title: 4. Check what it holds
docs.text:
service prometheus-exporter check
for p in $(pidof uhttpd); do grep -q handler.uc /proc/$p/cmdline && grep -E '^(RssAnon|VmData)' /proc/$p/status; done
free

check says the memory_limit the service runs under, and the collectors it serves. A collector that runs out of memory fails alone, with COLLECTOR_KILLED, and the exporter still serves the others. Raise memory_limit, or leave that collector out.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Performance on small routers: what a scrape costs, and what uhttpd holds.
  • Files and packages: what each package installs and depends on.
  • UCI configuration: memory_limit.

docs.title: How to Monitor SQM and CAKE
docs.text: The qdisc collector runs tc to read each network device's root queueing discipline (qdisc): what it sent, dropped and holds, with node_exporter's names. Where SQM shapes traffic with CAKE, the collector also reads CAKE's capacity and memory, and for each tin (CAKE's priority classes) its traffic, drops, ECN marks and delays.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • SQM is set up on the device, with cake as its queueing discipline (sqm-scripts, its layer_cake.qos or piece_of_cake.qos).

docs.title: 1. Install the qdisc collector
docs.text:
apk add ucode-prometheus-exporter-qdisc

It brings tc. The -network and -full groups also install it.

docs.title: 2. Find the devices SQM shapes
docs.text:
SQM makes CAKE the root qdisc of two devices: the interface it shapes, for upload, and an ifb4<device> it creates, for download:

prometheus-exporter scrape qdisc | grep '^node_qdisc_cake_capacity_estimate_bytes_per_second'

node_qdisc_cake_capacity_estimate_bytes_per_second{device="eth1"} 2500000
node_qdisc_cake_capacity_estimate_bytes_per_second{device="ifb4eth1"} 11875000

Here eth1 is the WAN's upload, shaped to 20 Mbit/s, and ifb4eth1 is its download, shaped to 95 Mbit/s.

docs.title: 3. Query it
docs.text:
Drops per second, by device and tin:

rate(node_qdisc_cake_tin_drops_total[5m])

The worst queueing delay of each tin, which SQM is there to keep low:

node_qdisc_cake_tin_peak_delay_seconds

The share of the shaped rate that the download uses (bytes per second over bytes per second):

rate(node_qdisc_bytes_total{device="ifb4eth1"}[5m])
  / on (device) node_qdisc_cake_capacity_estimate_bytes_per_second

ECN marks, which CAKE uses before it drops:

rate(node_qdisc_cake_tin_ecn_marks_total[5m])

Each tin is labeled by its index, as tc numbers them. A besteffort CAKE has only tin 0. A diffserv4 CAKE has tins 0 to 3, from Bulk to Voice.

docs.title: What it leaves out
docs.text:
The collector reads only the root qdisc of each device. So it leaves out:

  • SQM's ingress qdisc, which shapes nothing itself
  • a multiqueue NIC's per-queue children
  • HTB's leaves
  • noqueue, the qdisc of bridges, VLANs and WireGuard, whose counters are always 0

A device that SQM does not shape still shows its default qdisc, fq_codel, with node_qdisc_* and no node_qdisc_cake_*.

Metrics lists every family.

docs.title: How to Publish Metrics from Scripts
docs.text: The textfile collector serves the metrics of every *.prom file in a directory, /var/prometheus by default, as node_exporter's textfile collector does. A script on the device, run by cron or a hotplug event, writes its metrics there.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • ucode-prometheus-exporter-textfile, or the -full group, is installed.

docs.title: 1. Write the file
docs.text:
A file holds metrics in the Prometheus text format: # HELP and # TYPE lines, then samples. Write to a temporary file in the same directory, then rename it into place, so a scrape never reads half a file:

#!/bin/sh
# /usr/bin/apk-metrics: how many packages can be upgraded.
dir=/var/prometheus
tmp=$(mktemp "$dir/.apk.XXXXXX")
n=$(apk list --upgradable 2>/dev/null | wc -l)
cat >"$tmp" <<EOF
# HELP apk_upgradable_packages Packages with an upgrade available.
# TYPE apk_upgradable_packages gauge
apk_upgradable_packages $n
EOF
chmod 0644 "$tmp"
mv -f "$tmp" "$dir/apk.prom"

mktemp makes the file 0600, so only root can read it. The service reads it as its own user, prometheus-exporter, hence the chmod. The collector skips a file that only root can read, and logs it.

Some more rules for the file:

  • The temporary file's name must not end in .prom, or the collector reads it.
  • Write a regular file. The collector skips anything else (a FIFO, a device) without opening it, and counts it in node_textfile_scrape_error. So a pipe that nothing writes to cannot hold up a scrape.
  • Give your metrics names of your own. If a file writes metrics that another collector also writes (node_load1, for example), the whole textfile collector fails with FAMILY_CONFLICT.

docs.title: 2. Run it
docs.text:
From cron, every hour:

chmod +x /usr/bin/apk-metrics
echo '0 * * * * /usr/bin/apk-metrics' >>/etc/crontabs/root
service cron restart

docs.title: 3. Check it
docs.text:
prometheus-exporter scrape textfile

The output has the file's metrics, plus node_textfile_mtime_seconds{file="/var/prometheus/apk.prom"}, the time the file was last written, and node_textfile_scrape_error 0.

docs.title: If a file is left out
docs.text:
The collector leaves out a whole file if it:

  • cannot be read,
  • is not valid text format,
  • gives a family a different type than an earlier file did,
  • repeats a series an earlier file has, or
  • writes one of textfile's own families.

node_textfile_scrape_error is then 1, and the log says which file and why:

logread -e prometheus-exporter | grep textfile

daemon.warn prometheus-exporter[1]: collector 'textfile': skipped /var/prometheus/apk.prom: EXPOSITION_INVALID (line 3: ...)

The collector itself still succeeds. Alert on node_textfile_scrape_error == 1. Also alert when node_textfile_mtime_seconds is too old for how often the script runs.

docs.title: Use another directory
docs.text:
uci set prometheus-exporter.textfile=collector
uci set prometheus-exporter.textfile.directory=/var/lib/metrics
uci commit prometheus-exporter
service prometheus-exporter reload

The directory must be under /var, /tmp or /etc/prometheus-exporter, and must not be one that every service shares, such as /var/run. When the service starts, it creates the directory as root if it is missing, and mounts it in its jail. So it refuses any other directory, with OWNED_DIRECTORY.

Keep the directory on tmpfs (/var, /tmp). Only if the metrics must survive a reboot, put it under /etc/prometheus-exporter: a script that writes to flash wears it out.

docs.title: How to Troubleshoot
docs.text: Start from what is wrong: the service, one collector, or the scrape as Prometheus sees it. Each section below covers one case.

docs.title: The service does not run
docs.text:
Browser (LuCI)Terminal (SSH)

Open Status → Prometheus exporter. A banner above the tables says whether the exporter is enabled but not running, or switched off in its settings. Its System log button opens Status → System Log: look for the lines with prometheus-exporter.

service prometheus-exporter status
logread -e prometheus-exporter

If the exporter is switched off, turn it on: in LuCI, tick Enable on the General tab of Services → Prometheus exporter and press Save & Apply, or use the SSH commands in the table's first row.

status or the log says Do disabled (option enabled in /etc/config/prometheus-exporter) uci set prometheus-exporter.main.enabled=1, commit, service prometheus-exporter start. invalid configuration, not starting, after the lines that say why Fix the option it names: service prometheus-exporter check shows the same as FAIL lines. See UCI configuration. deferring start until listen interface <name> becomes ready The interface has no address yet. It starts once it has one; check ifstatus <name>, or listen elsewhere: How to listen on the LAN. basic auth takes HTTPS only, and <cert> or <key> is missing: not starting The TLS files are not there. See How to serve HTTPS with basic auth. cannot make <path>: <error> The service could not make a directory: tmpfs is full, or the path is wrong.

If you reload with an invalid configuration, the service keeps the running exporter and logs invalid configuration, keeping the running instance.

docs.title: A collector fails
docs.text:
Run a scrape, and see for each collector whether it succeeded, failed, or had nothing to observe, and why:

Browser (LuCI)Terminal (SSH)

Open Status → Prometheus exporter. Failed collectors come first. Test run says Failed with why and its error code, or Nothing to observe with why.

service prometheus-exporter check

warn scrape: dnsmasq: UBUS_CALL_FAILED (dnsmasq metrics: Not found)
ok   scrape: wifi has nothing to observe: no wireless radios
  • Nothing to observe is not a failure. It means the device lacks the hardware, kernel feature or running service the collector reads. The collector succeeds without samples, and its node_scrape_collector_observing is 0. If you do not want the collector, disable it. Collectors lists when each collector has nothing to observe.

  • A failure has a code: a warn line of check, or Failed in LuCI. Error codes says what each code means. Under procd, the service also logs each failing scrape at warning:

    logread -e prometheus-exporter | grep "collector '"

The ubus object's status shows the same:

ubus call prometheus-exporter status

docs.title: A collector is quarantined
docs.text:
The service quarantines a collector when:

  • the exporter killed its program at its timeout,
  • it was still running at the end of its budget (the time it may take),
  • its process ended under it, or
  • it failed three scrapes in a row.

The service then leaves the collector out for a few scrapes, and tries it again. Meanwhile, its node_scrape_collector_success is 0 and its ucode_prometheus_exporter_collector_quarantined is 1. check says why, and when the service tries it again:

warn service: nat_traffic is quarantined: COLLECTOR_OVERRUN (took 7.84 s, over its budget of 5 s); the service tries it again in 8 scrapes, or at once once restarted
  1. Fix what tripped it. check runs the collector now, and its warn scrape: line says how it fails.
  2. If the collector is slow but you want it, raise its budget. In LuCI, press Edit on its row of the Collectors tab, set Budget, press Save, then Save & Apply. Over SSH: uci set prometheus-exporter.<module>=collector, uci set prometheus-exporter.<module>.budget=15, commit, reload_config. If a program is slow, raise its timeout: see How to give programs more time.
  3. To try it at once rather than wait for its trial, run service prometheus-exporter restart. A restart forgets every quarantine.

LuCI's Status → Prometheus exporter page shows the same in its Service's scrapes column, and names the quarantined collectors in a notice above the tables. The exporter collector counts quarantines since the service started, in ucode_prometheus_exporter_quarantines_total{collector}.

docs.title: A collector breaks the contract
docs.text:
The log says collector '<name>': followed by one of the errors below. Only that collector fails. The exporter serves every other collector as before.

Error What happened Do COLLECTOR_CANCELLED It was still running at the end of its budget, and was stopped with its process: a loop that never ends, or a read that never returns (a FIFO, a socket). If it is only slow, raise its budget; otherwise it is a bug of the collector. COLLECTOR_KILLED Its process ended under it: past the memory limit, a crash, exit(); or its scrape process died while it ran, collector '<name>' was running when a scrape process died. Raise memory_limit if it is only large; otherwise it is a bug. SAMPLE_LIMIT It wrote more than its max_samples: the detail says how many, and in which family. If its output is that large on this device, raise its max_samples. EXPOSITION_INVALID It wrote what Prometheus would refuse the whole scrape for: a label value or HELP text that is not valid UTF-8 (a Latin-1 SSID or hostname), or two label names that are one once sanitized. The detail names the family and the label. A bug of the collector, which should make the value valid or leave it out. FAMILY_CONFLICT It wrote a family another collector writes, or one the exporter keeps for itself: the detail names it. Disable one of the two, or fix the collector's names. hung at load (at err) Its module's top level did not return in 5 s: it is left out until the service restarts. A bug of the module. COLLECTOR_IMPURE (at err) Its module's top level called what only collect() may, as sleep() or print(): it is left out until the service restarts. prometheus-exporter collector check <file> names the line. A bug of the module: see The top level.

prometheus-exporter collector check <module file> (from ucode-prometheus-exporter-cli) runs a module as the service would, and says which rule it breaks: see Collector contract.

docs.title: Collectors are left out at the deadline
docs.text:
A scrape ran out of the time the scraper gives it. The log says scrape deadline: <n> collectors not served in its <seconds> s: ..., and check says the scrape deadline left <name> out. Collectors run fastest first, so the ones left out are the slowest.

  • Leave the slow collector out of this job, with params: { 'exclude[]': [ nat_traffic ] }. Scrape it in a job of its own with a longer scrape_timeout, and a budget to match.
  • Or raise the job's scrape_timeout. Prometheus sends it with each scrape.
  • If a scraper does not send X-Prometheus-Scrape-Timeout-Seconds, the exporter uses the main section's scrape_timeout, 10 seconds.
  • ucode_prometheus_exporter_deadline_skips_total{collector} counts the skips since the service started.

See About deadlines and circuit breakers.

docs.title: A collector works in check and fails under procd
docs.text:
check, the ubus object's status, LuCI's status page and prometheus-exporter scrape run the collectors in the service's own jail, as Prometheus's scrapes do. So they see what Prometheus gets.

Where ujail cannot run, they run the collectors outside the jail, as root, and check says scrape, outside the jail. A collector that works there and fails under procd needs something the jail does not give it.

  1. See what the jail gives it:

    service prometheus-exporter check | grep '^warn jail'
ubus call service list '{"name":"prometheus-exporter"}'

    check warns about a path or program it cannot mount. procd's list shows what it mounted.

  2. If a path was missing when the service started, the service mounts it once it appears. check says <path> is not there; the service mounts it once it is, and the watch instance reloads the service when the path appears. To mount it at once, run service prometheus-exporter restart.

  3. A program that is not installed shows as a jail: <collector>: command <name> is not on ... warning. Install its package.

The jail lists what the jail holds.

docs.title: Prometheus cannot scrape it
docs.text: Prometheus says Do connection refused The exporter does not listen where Prometheus asks. service prometheus-exporter status says where it listens; by default, loopback only. See How to listen on the LAN. A timeout The firewall drops it, or the scrape is slow: the exporter answers within the timeout the scraper sends, but not on the first scrape after a restart, before it knows how long each collector takes. A timeout scrape after scrape is a scraper that sends none: set scrape_timeout to its timeout. 400 Bad Request The scrape's collect[] names a collector that is not installed, or is disabled. The body says which. 401 Unauthorized The user or password is wrong. server returned HTTP status 403 Forbidden Basic auth is on and the request came over HTTP: use scheme: https. 500 Internal Server Error Basic auth's file is broken, or gone while auth_user is set: service prometheus-exporter restart writes it afresh.

docs.title: The metrics are not what you expect
docs.text:
• A name differs from the feed's exporters: see Renamed metrics.
  • A label is missing: a collector leaves out a label it has no value for.
  • Counters that are 0 are missing: option omit_zero_values '1' leaves them out.
  • To see how the scrape went, read what each collector reports about itself: node_scrape_collector_success is 0 for a failure, node_scrape_collector_observing is 0 for nothing to observe, and node_scrape_collector_duration_seconds is the time each took.

This query alerts on a failing collector, and ignores one with nothing to observe:

node_scrape_collector_success == 0

The bundled rules alert on it, and on the rest of the exporter's health: see How to monitor a router with the bundled dashboards and alerts.

docs.title: How to Monitor Unbound
docs.text: The unbound collector reads Unbound's statistics from its control socket, a Unix socket. OpenWrt's unbound package does not create one, so you turn it on, at the path the collector looks for.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Unbound runs on the device (unbound-daemon), enabled.
  • ucode-prometheus-exporter-unbound is installed. It brings ucode-mod-socket.

docs.title: 1. Give Unbound a control socket
docs.text:
Add to /etc/unbound/unbound_ext.conf:

remote-control:
    control-enable: yes
    control-interface: /var/lib/unbound/unbound.ctl

Then restart Unbound:

service unbound restart

The package creates /var/lib/unbound for Unbound alone. Unbound creates the socket there when it starts.

docs.title: 2. Check it
docs.text:
ls -l /var/lib/unbound/unbound.ctl
prometheus-exporter scrape unbound | grep unbound_queries_total

The service mounts the socket's directory in its jail. At boot, Unbound starts after the exporter. The service mounts the directory a few seconds after Unbound creates it, and the scrapes before that fail. Until then, check warns:

warn jail: unbound: /var/lib/unbound is not there; the service mounts it once it is

docs.title: Extended statistics
docs.text:
With extended-statistics: yes, Unbound counts more:

  • the queries by type, class, opcode, header flag and transport
  • the answers by rcode and DNSSEC result
  • the caches' entries and memory, and the modules' memory
  • a histogram of the recursion times

OpenWrt's package sets it from the UCI option extended_stats:

uci set unbound.ub_main.extended_stats=1
uci commit unbound
service unbound restart

Once the reply has them, the collector writes them with letsencrypt/unbound_exporter's names: unbound_query_types_total{type}, unbound_answer_rcodes_total{rcode}, unbound_response_time_seconds and the rest. See Metrics. Keeping these counts costs Unbound some time per query, which is why the package leaves them off.

Unbound leaves out a query type, class, opcode or rcode that no query has had yet (stat_inhibit_zero). Those series appear as the queries arrive.

The collector leaves out what unbound_exporter does not export: the memory of the stream and HTTP buffers (mem.streamwait, mem.http.*) and the caches' lock collisions (*.max_collisions). For an Unbound built with DNSCrypt, it also leaves out every DNSCrypt statistic, including mem.cache.dnscrypt_*, which unbound_exporter would write as two more caches.

docs.title: Use another socket
docs.text:
If Unbound's socket is elsewhere, tell the collector:

uci set prometheus-exporter.unbound=collector
uci set prometheus-exporter.unbound.socket=/var/lib/unbound/control.sock
uci commit prometheus-exporter
service prometheus-exporter reload

The jail mounts the socket's directory, never the socket itself. That directory must be Unbound's own. The service refuses a directory that every service shares, such as /run or /var/run, and the collector then cannot reach the socket.

The jail also holds everything else in that directory, read-only. In /var/lib/unbound, that is Unbound's generated config and root.key, and the TLS keys of unbound-control if its setup created them.

docs.title: If it fails
docs.text: check or the log says Cause unbound has nothing to observe: unbound is disabled Unbound's init script is disabled. Nothing is wrong. SOCKET_FAILED (/var/lib/unbound/unbound.ctl: ... No such file or directory) No socket: step 1 is missing, or Unbound has not restarted. SOCKET_FAILED (...: no reply for 1000 ms) Unbound did not answer in a second.

docs.title: Remove a collector
docs.text:
Browser (LuCI)Terminal (SSH)
  1. Open System → Software, and type the package's name in Filter, such as ucode-prometheus-exporter-wifi.
  2. On the Installed tab, press Remove… on its row, then Remove in the dialog.
apk del ucode-prometheus-exporter-wifi

The service reloads without it. You cannot remove a collector of the base package this way: disable it instead. A collector that a group installed stays while the group is installed. Remove the group, or keep the group and disable the collector.

docs.title: Remove the exporter
docs.text:
Remove the base package and everything that depends on it: the collector packages, the groups and the LuCI app:

apk del -r ucode-prometheus-exporter

The service stops, and rpcd no longer serves the prometheus-exporter ubus object. If you changed /etc/config/prometheus-exporter, apk keeps it. Remove it if you do not want it:

rm -f /etc/config/prometheus-exporter

What the service created at run time, /var/run/prometheus-exporter/ and textfile's /var/prometheus/, is on tmpfs and disappears at the next reboot. The service's ubus ACL goes when the service stops.

The user and group prometheus-exporter stay, as OpenWrt keeps every package's user, but with nothing granted. When the package is removed, the service stops, and on stopping it:

  • gives back the original group and mode of each config and /proc file it opened to that group, and
  • takes the user out of every other group.

If Prometheus scrapes the device, remove it from the scrape configuration, or its target stays down.

docs.title: How to Upgrade the Exporter
docs.text: Upgrade every exporter package together. Each collector package, each group, the command line's package and the LuCI app depends on the base package of exactly the same version.

docs.title: Before you upgrade
docs.text: Read what the new version changes. Before 0.3.0, a minor version could rename metrics or options. From 0.3.0 on, only a major version does: see About versions. A renamed metric breaks every query and dashboard that uses the old name.

docs.title: From the feed
docs.text:
If you added the exporter's feed, as How to install the exporter does, run:

apk update
apk upgrade

docs.title: From .apk files
docs.text:
1. Copy the new version of every package you have installed to the device's /tmp.
  2. Set version to the new version, as the files' names end, and add them all in one command:
version=0.2.0-r1
apk add --allow-untrusted /tmp/ucode-prometheus-exporter-*$version.apk /tmp/luci-app-prometheus-exporter-$version.apk

Adding the base package alone fails, because the installed collectors still want the old version.

If the new version adds a dependency, apk takes it from the feeds the device has. For example, ucode-docopt, which the command line's package depends on, comes from the exporter's feed.

docs.title: From 0.2.1 to 0.3.0
docs.text:
0.3.0 is the first release candidate for 1.0: 1.0 keeps its metrics, options, methods and collector API, as About versions lists them. The changes below break something that worked in 0.2.1. The CHANGELOG marks each one BREAKING.

  • snmp6 exports 13 fields of each device by default, where 0.2.1 wrote every one, some 70. By default it now keeps only these node_snmp6_*_total fields of each device: Ip6_InOctets, Ip6_OutOctets, Ip6_OutForwDatagrams, Ip6_InDiscards, Ip6_OutDiscards, Ip6_InNoRoutes, Ip6_OutNoRoutes, Ip6_InHdrErrors, Ip6_InAddrErrors, Ip6_InTooBigErrors, Icmp6_InMsgs, Icmp6_OutMsgs and Icmp6_InErrors. It also drops node_snmp6_ifindex, since netclass's node_network_iface_id has the same index. To export other fields, set the new option fields, a regular expression of <Protocol>_<Field>. .* exports every field, as 0.2.1 did:

    uci set prometheus-exporter.snmp6=collector
uci set prometheus-exporter.snmp6.fields='.*'
uci commit prometheus-exporter

  • nat_traffic writes one series per host on this side of the router, labeled host. 0.2.1 wrote one series per pair of addresses, labeled src and dst. So node_nat_traffic_bytes{src,dst} is now node_nat_traffic_bytes{host}.

    host is the end of the connection that is on this side of the router, a LAN host or the router itself, as the routes say:

    • For a LAN host's connection out, it is the source, as src was.
    • For a port-forwarded connection, it is the LAN host the connection reaches. src was the remote address.
    • For a connection from the internet to the router, it is the router's WAN address. For ICMPv6 to a LAN host, it is the LAN host. In both cases src was the sender.

    Connections with neither end on this side share one series, host="other". So do the hosts beyond the 2048 with the most bytes.

    A query by src becomes a query by host, as node_nat_traffic_bytes{host="192.168.1.10"}. A query by dst needs the pairs. The new option peers brings them back, labeled host and peer. It writes as many series as 0.2.1 did, with new ones for every connection, and a Prometheus server keeps each for hours. Turn it on only for a short look:

    uci set prometheus-exporter.nat_traffic=collector
uci set prometheus-exporter.nat_traffic.peers=1
uci commit prometheus-exporter

  • cert and key must be under /etc/ssl, /etc/acme or /etc/prometheus-exporter, or be uhttpd's own /etc/uhttpd.*. Each must be a regular file of at most 64 KiB. If it is a link, the link must stay inside those directories. Root copies these files for the service's group, and copies no others. The service refuses a configuration that names another path (TLS_PATH), such as /etc/prometheus-exporter.crt, which this guide's HTTPS how-to used. It does not start until you move the files, as check says:

    mkdir -p /etc/prometheus-exporter
mv /etc/prometheus-exporter.crt /etc/prometheus-exporter/tls.crt
mv /etc/prometheus-exporter.key /etc/prometheus-exporter/tls.key
uci set prometheus-exporter.main.cert=/etc/prometheus-exporter/tls.crt
uci set prometheus-exporter.main.key=/etc/prometheus-exporter/tls.key
uci commit prometheus-exporter

    The configuration import from a feed exporter leaves out such a cert or key, and logs it: option cert: expected a file under /etc/ssl, ...; left at the default. See How to serve HTTPS with basic auth. - The jail no longer runs as root. uhttpd runs in it as the user and group prometheus-exporter, which the upgrade creates. The upgrade restarts a running service. On start, the service grants that user what its enabled collectors declare. You need to do nothing: - The state directory belongs to the user, and starts empty, as at every restart. - The service writes basic auth's file again, readable by the user's group. - The service copies the TLS key and certificate for the user's group. The original files stay as they were, the key readable by root alone. - The service opens the configs its collectors read to the user's group, read-only.

    See The jail. - textfile's files must be readable by the service's user. If a script writes a *.prom file that only root can read (mode 0600, as mktemp makes it), textfile skips the file and logs it. Run chmod 0644 on the file before renaming it into place. See How to publish metrics from scripts. - The prometheus-exporter command is now its own package, ucode-prometheus-exporter-cli. The base package no longer installs /usr/bin/prometheus-exporter, and no longer depends on ucode-docopt. So apk upgrade leaves the device without the command. A script or cron job that runs it fails until you install the package. That includes prometheus-exporter scrape, which How to push metrics uses, and hash-password:

    apk add ucode-prometheus-exporter-cli

    The service does not need the command: - service prometheus-exporter check, and the check that start and reload run, are the base package's /usr/libexec/prometheus-exporter/check.uc. - LuCI and the ubus object set basic auth's password (set_password).

    Without the command's package, apk also removes ucode-docopt, which nothing else of the exporter needs. See The prometheus-exporter command. - A collector of another package that calls ubus must declare its calls in meta.ubus, as ubus: { dnsmasq: [ 'metrics' ], rc: [ 'list' ] } (rc list for the API's services). The loader refuses a collector that needs ubus without them, and a call the collector does not declare fails with UBUS_NOT_ALLOWED.
